speechtext: That in accordance with the recommendations contained in the first report of the select standing committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills, the time for receiving petitions for private bills be renewed until Wednesday April 14 next, and that that portion of rule 89 which limits the time for filing private bills be suspended for the present session.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR RECEIVING PETITIONS AND FILING BILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this motion was before the House yesterday I asked that it might stand until I had had time to ascertain exactly what it involved. The Internal Economy Commission has reported on the question, and I purpose to place its report on Hansard so that the House with this report before it may share responsibility with the Private Bills committee if this motion is agreed to. This is the commission's report:
The Commission of Internal Economy of the House of Commons held a meeting this morning and took up the question of remitting fines to such applicants for private bills as did not present their petitions within the delays fixed by the niles.
The Private Bills committee report, read in the House yesterday, recommended that the time for receiving petitions which expired on February 18 last 14011-119i	[DOT]
be extended until Wednesday, April 14, next, and that rule 89 be suspended in relation thereto. A motion for concurrence in this report is to be made this afternoon. The Clerk of the House has pointed out that under this rule a fine of $200 is levied on all bills introduced after the twelfth week of the session. There are at the present time a large number of divorce bills and several incorporation bills for which the delays have expired. As we have 175 divorce bills so far, most of which have come too late, and several companies' solicitors have informed us that they intend to apply for legislation, I may safely say, after consultation with the officers of the House, that the aggregate amount of fees and fines thus remitted would be approximately $20,000.
In the case of companies, the promoters avoid paying a large fee by introducing their bills in the Senate, where they are only called upon to pay $300 whether they are late or not. When the bill comes before the Commons a net fine of $200 is charged because a petition has not been duly filed. In this way the country makes $500 on that particular bill.
The Commission of Internal Economy went into the matter very thoroughly, and heard Mr. Walter Todd, GiB0i oi tue rrivaie .dims oianch, who represented that such a report as the one presented yesterday by the chairman of the committee had not been- made to the House for the past fifteen years. It has been the custom to consider each case on its own merits.
Moreover, it is no fault of parliament if the applicants for private legislation are late in presenting their petitions. Sufficient notice of the opening of the session was given to the general public; shortly after the general election it was officially announced that parliament would be called for December 10-the proclamation calling the session for January 7 was published in the Canada Gazette on December 1.
There does not seem to be any valuable reason why petitioners should not have 'been ready in time. It is certainly not the fault of the House of Commons if they are late, and the commissioners were of the opinion that parliament should not be penaflized under the circumstances.
I direct what follows to the particular attention of my hon. friend (Mr. Parent):
The principle that whoever is responsible for the delays should pay the costs was accepted as the best solution in the matter.
Heretofore parliament has considered each case on its merits, and I submit to my hon. friend that he might very well point out to the Private Bills committee the practice which is usually followed in such cases. It seems to me that the Private Bills committee, fairly representative of both sides of the House, has not carefully considered how this wholesale proposal will affect the public revenues.

I heard a report, rather

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF RIGHT HON. GEORGE P. GRAHAM AS CHAIRMAN
speechtext:
I am sure that both the
House and the country will be gratified to learn that the government, after very con-oiderable persuasion, has succeeded m obtaining the consent of the Right Hon. George P. Graham to become chairman of the proposed tariff board. Mr. Graham was anxious to have a brief space of well earned rest, but acting from a sense of public duty he has listened to the very strong representations of members of the administration and has agreed to the postponement, for a time at least, of the opportunity of recreation for which he was preparing, and to accept immediately the position of chairman of the board. I feel I am only expressing what hon. members of the House will generally concede, that with the wealth of experience which Mr. Graham will bring to the conduct of the affairs of the board he will succeed in having it organized and functioning sucessfully at an early date. I believe I voice a general sentiment when I express the hope that he will see his way clear to occupy the chairmanship of the board for a long time to come.
The government's intention is not to have a large board, but one limited in numbers, giving to the board, however, power to engage, from time to time, experts to assist it in its work. Naturally, in connection with a subject so technical as the tariff, the board will desire to have the fullest information from the best available sources, and accurate interpretation; and the government has thought that a board comparatively limited in numbers enjoying the power in association with itself to secure from different parts of the country and from various sources expert advice and opinion, would be better than a large board formed in an attempt to represent all phases and possible interests. A small body, thus empowered can, it is believed, more effectively deal with the questions that will come before it than a larger and more cumbersome permanent organization. The membership of the board has accordingly been limited' to three. The Right Hon. Mr. Graham will, as I have said, be chairman and the other two members will be Mr. Joseph Daoust, ex-President of the Chamber of Commerce of Montreal, and Mr. Donald Gordon McKenzie, from Brandon, Manitoba, a well known farmer of the west. I may observe that, associated with these gentlemen, there will be a number of the members of the permanent service, chosen from various departments of the government. The Departments of Finance, Customs, Trade and Commerce, Agriculture, Labour and External Affairs and the Statistical branch will doubtless make their contributions as required. These departments all possess able public servants who have special knowledge that will be of great utility to the board in the discharge of its duties. These public servants will co-operate with the board in its work. There will also be a permanent secretary to the 'board. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) informs me that the gentleman whose name I was just about to mention has not yet formally signified his acceptance of the position. However, I hope on Monday next to lay on the table of the House a copy of the order in council setting forth in full the personnel and powers of the board.

Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Acting Minister of Immigration, a-nd Colonization) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to authorize advances to settlers on crown lands, and to provide,-
l.That for purposes connected with settlement, the minister may make loans to settlers on the basis of improvement of land and farm buildings erected-(a) to a settler who is a Canadian citizen as that term is defined in the Immigration Act, an amount not exceeding $1,000, (b) to a settler other than a Canadian citizen an amount not exceeding $500.

2.	That settlement loans under the proposed legislation shall not exceed the sum of $5,000,000 in any fiscal year, and shall be paid out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund.
3.	That Settlement Loan committees may be established anywhere in Canada to report upon and recommend to the minister the suitability of a settler, and of any parcel of crown land, and to advise the minister as to the amount of loan to be made and how it should be expended, and such committee shall consist of not less than two nor more than three persons in the employ of the Dominion government or of any provincial government, such persons to be nominated by the minister, one of whom shall be the Dominion lands agent or the provincial crown lands agent, as the case may be, for the district in which the settler is located, and no salary or remuneration additional to that which he otherwise receives shall be paid to members of such committee.
4.	That no settlement loan shall be made unless recommended by a Settlement Loan committee, and unless approved by the minister, nor until the applicant has been recommended by a committee as a suitable settler and the iand as suitable for settlement for agricultural purposes, and all settlement loans shall be expended under the direction of the minister.
5.	That no settlement loan shall be made upon the security of improvements upon any provincial crown land, unless the province by appropriate legislation, has provided that the improvements upon the security of which any such loan is made shall be subject to a first charge for the amount of such loan with interest, and that no patent shall be issued for the said land until such loan with interest is repaid in full.
6.	That the payment of principal shall be made in annual instalments extending over a period of not more than ten years from the date the settlement loan is made, the first payment to become due and payable two years from the date of the settlement, loan, provided that the settler may at any time repay the whole of the settlement loan with interest to date of payment, and all loans shall bear interest at the rate of five per cent per annum, payable on the respective dates upon which instalments of principal fall due.
7.	That when a settlement loan has been made upon the security of improvements upon Dominion crown lands, the patent shall not issue until the loan and all interest charges thereon have been paid in full.
8.	That if a provincial government, not having suitable crown lands available, acquires by purchase suitable lands for settlement under the provisions of this legislation, the minister may pay to a provincial government a sum not exceeding one-half of the interest on the purchase price of such lands, reckoned at five per centum per annum, for a period not exceeding two years from the date of settlement.
9.	That the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the minister, make regulations to carry out these provisions, and the minister shall make an annual report to parliament of all operations under the proposed legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
The bill is
a new departure in the encouragement of immigration. In the old days, when we had a large influx of settlers to the lands of western Canada, there were lying adjacent to all

Advances lo Settlers
the railway lines lands that were known as homestead lands, and these were available to every individual who could qualify under the regulations. There is still a large quantity of land, though not of first-class quality, lying not so much in the southern portion of the prairie provinces, nor indeed in the southern portion of Ontario, but throughout all the provinces of Canada with the exception of the Maritime provinces there is a considerable area of crown lands, provincial crown lands and Dominion crown lands, lying within a radius of fifteen miles of existing railway lines. These lands, of course, are not as desirable as the lands taken up in former days by applicants who were desirous of settling upon them and developing farms in the various provinces, but particularly in the western provinces. For various reasons these crown 1 mi els arc still available and one of tl*e problems that the Immigration department have to face is the fact that if open lands, and there are still open lands available in western Canada, are to be procured by the newcomers or by those who under the regulations can homestead our crown lands, they would have to go a very considerable distance back from the present railway facilities, which would involve on the part of the provinces the construction of roads and of schools, and so far as the federal government is concerned, it invariably involves the building of new railway lines. I think most members of the House will agree with me that what we ought to try to do is to consolidate our settlement along the existing lines of railway which have been built and are now in operation, and which have already been financed. In all the three prairie provinces these lands are very largely covered, if not with timber, with a very heavy growth of underbrush, and are somewhat difficult to bring under cultivation without entailing a considerable amount of labour. That was the thought in my mind when I recommended to the government the adoption of this policy for the settlement of crown lands. In most of those settlements to-day, while perhaps there are not school-houses, there are to some extent facilities by way of roads, because the idea is not to locate the settler beyond a point from which he can travel to his nearest railway centre, nor to involve expenditure by the provincial governments or by the federal government for improvements necessary to open up entirely new areas. That is the object that was in my mind when I recommended to the government this policy of assistance to the settler going on these new lands.
Perhaps the House will be surprised to know that we have in Manitoba almost three million acres of land still available for settlement coming within the category I have mentioned. In Saskatchewan well over one million acres, and in Alberta well over six million acres; so there is a very considerable amount of crown lands available for settlement lying contiguous to the railway lines already in existence and in operation. Now, these are not all first class lands, no one would make that claim. In the case of a considerable proportion they are, perhaps lands not desirable for settlement. But in the case of the three prairie provinces, there is a very large area of lands very suitable for agriculture lying within the fifteen mile limit. In the old days of homesteading in the west, when millions of dollars were being poured into the country by the various railway companies for the construction of new lines of railway, there was a certain popular form of obtaining sufficient money to carry the settler along. I think I am safe in making the statement that in 95 per cent of the cases the homesteaders who went upon the land were men without means, men who undertook to live upon those lands for six months in the year doing what they could and spending the remaining six months in earning what was called in those days a grubstake to carry them over the next period. As I say, employment was easy to ibe had. Vast sums of money were being expended throughout the west at that time particularly in railway building and also in the construction of buildings and the opening up of new towns. Therefore no difficulty was experienced at that time in obtaining employment. To-day the man who goes upon a homestead may find temporary employment in assisting with the harvesting operations in the older settled areas, or in working for a farmer who is already established. But that class of employment can only be obtained in the summer season when the settler can be most advantageously employed in improving his own holding. In endeavouring to find a solution for this problem we thought we could hold out hope of assistance to the individual who would settle upon the land; that as he improved his holding, as he progressed in the construction of his buildings, in the erection of his little home -it might be of log construction and very likely it will; many of us who went out on the prairies first were content with sod construction because we were unable to buy lumber for the building of our home-the new settler would be able by making application to the board to secure an allowance to be applied to the cost, materials and construction. This will enable him to provide for the neces-
Advances to Settlers

sities of life and if he is fortunately situated, he can devote some portion of the advance to the purchase of machinery. As he improves his land and buildings further advances will be made to him up to a maximum of SI,000. The idea is to prevent people who desire to own land from locating in the extreme areas of settlement instead of near the railway, and to give them the assistance they will need in the pioneer years when they are endeavouring to establish homes for themselves. It will be a tremendous advantage to the settlers themselves to have this consolidation of settlement along the railway line.
The committee will notice that some difference is being made between Canadians and people who come from countries outside of Canada. For some considerable time past there has been an agitation to bring people from the urban centres of the Dominion back to the land. It is an undeniable fact that a great many desirable agriculturists have left our farm lands and migrated into towns and cities. The best evidence of that is to be found in the statistical information in our possession, which shows that to-day, perhaps, more than 50 per cent of our people are residing in ufiban centres, notwithstanding the fact that Canada is an agricultural country. I am not so well informed as to the conditions in eastern Canada, but I do know that in the west a great many of our people who are now residing in the cities would be glad of an opportunity to go back to the land and try to establish themselves again in agricultural pursuits rather than remain as wage-earners in the city.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Does not
this apply principally to the prairie provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Principally
but not altogether. I will explain later how it applies to the older provinces. There are many cases of young men, sons of farmers, who are desirous of going out and establishing homes for themselves. A loan to them at 5 per cent will assist them very materially in obtaining a grant of land by way of homesteading, improving that land and making homes for themselves. So, the Canadian government proposes to make a loan to a maximum of $1,000 to citizens of the character I have described.
To those who come to Canada as immigrants the proposal is to lend them $500, not the full $1,000 to assist them in establishing themselves upon the land.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
How long after they
arrive in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Of necessity they would have to establish themselves before they could make application for the loan. If they did that during the first year they could make the application then; but the act provides that they must be upon a homestead within fifteen miles of an existing railway, and there must be evidence on their part that they have made improvements. It was felt that some difference should be made between those who come to us as immigrants and our own people. For that reason we do not propose to make as great a loan to the former class as to our own citizens. I think it can be said that iu the case of these immigrants the conditions they have left are not as favourable as those they will encounter in Canada, and therefore they will be able to get along with a lesser amount than our own citizens. I am able to sireak from personal knowledge of the adaptability of many of those who come from outside countries. I know that in my own province of Alberta one of the most prosperous settlements to-day is the Ukrainian settlement established around the town of Vegreville. Those people when they first came in brought everything they owned in a sack; and I am sure the members for Edmonton and the surrounding districts will bear me out when I say that there are in the Dominion no finer farms and none with more up-to-date equipment than in that particular district after eighteen or twenty years of settlement by the Ukrainians. And that has been done by our Scandinavian settlers and many people who have come from countries foreign to Canada and taken up their residence among them. We felt that some difference should be made, that we owed something to our own people in this respect, and that we should endeavour to be a little more generous to our own people than we would to those of foreign extraction who were coming to our country to establish themselves. In the case of the Britisher who comes here, of course our hope is that we will be able to interest the Overseas Settlement Board, and that they will make a loan to the British settler identical with that obtained by the Canadian. We are in joint operation with the British government on a good many schemes, more particularly that of the migration of 3.000 families to whom we are supplying land; the British government putting up in cash $1,500 for the establishment of those people upon our land, and that is working out very satisfactorily. We hope this year that we shall establish 1,200 British families in that way upon the soldier settlement land that we now are holding for this purpose.

Advances to Settlers

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: One of the difficulties in the west, as my hon. friend knows, is with the municipalities which have a large quantity of unpatented land. They cannot sell those lands for arrears of taxes. maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I do not want to get into a controversy about this matter in regard to the crown paying taxes,
Advances to Settlers

because I expect it will come up at a later date, but I think it should be borne in mind that it would be a very serious matter for the crown to have to agree to pay taxes on land held by the crown. While the settler is in occupation there will be no serious difficulty about the collection of taxes, so far as the soldier settler is concerned. As a matter of fact to-day, until the date of abandonment, the crown has protected the municipality in the school district, but at the moment of abandonment when the land reverts to the crown, it is then in a different category, and there are very serious difficulties about any suggestion of the crown being responsible for the payment of those taxes while it is strictly crown land, and naturally the same difficulty will apply here, because it would be general in its application. If you could confine it to any particular case it would not be so bad, but the breaking away in any particular instance would create what my hon. friends speak of so often as a precedent. I fear it would work very detrimentally to the crown, and I would much rather find some other way of solving the difficulty. My desire is to help the municipalities to increase settlement within their boundaries and so long as the settler is on the land they will have the same right to collect taxes that they would have under the Homestead Act as it stands to-day.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: These are lands that would be open for homesteading under ordinary circumstances?

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

I think we

Mr. MoGIBBON: How long would a man have to be on the land before he qualified for a loan?

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

go on and expend the money in any way you wish or even under instructions, but rather to lend him money after he has made progress in improvements or in building and there is justification for the issue of a proportionate amount of the loan..

is going to lend money on its own security.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

speechtext:

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:

Mr. HANNESSO'N: Would it be possible to give this assistance under the Rural Credits bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: I think not. The Rural Credits bill is of an entirely different character. It is intended to deal with men who have patents for their land or, in other words, who are private owners.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

Mr. MoGIBBON:	What ground is there

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will look at the earnings of our railways, he will notice that years of surplus are always those when agriculturists have had good crops. iMore money is put into circulation when there is prosperity among agriculturists than in years of dearth. The idea in thickening up the agriculturist population along our railway lines is that this will help to lessen the deficits on our railways by creating more traffic, more business in the country. If that were not so, I would oppose a loan of any sort.

Advances to Settlers

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: May I remind the minister of Sir Henry Thornton's statement that the falling off in the earnings of the railways was due to the falling off in the manufactures of this country, and the return made to this House which I placed on Hansard a few weeks ago showed that wheat in the west was being carried at a loss by the railways?

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Being a
westerner I would not like to admit that.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Those were not my
figures; they were the figures of the minister's own government.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
All I can
say in reply to my hon. friend is that my observation goes to show that when you have, not particularly a big wheat crop, because that is confined very largely to western Canada, but a good agricultural crop throughout Canada, you have a year of great prosperity in the country. I think my hon. friend will not deny that statement. I am not denying for a moment the fact
4 p.m. that industry plays a very important part in the matter. My hon. friend will realize, however, that boards of trade in a'll the important cities in Canada are crying out for more immigrants. Where do they want these immigrants to go? They want them to go on the land, and our difficulty is to find, in countries from which we recruit settlers, people with money to establish themselves. If we could secure from the Old Land and the continent people with means bo establish themselves on the land, we would have no necessity for a bill to give assistance of this character. If we had former conditions in the way of employment on account of the expansion of the railways as we had in past years in western Canada, there would not be so much necessity for such a bill. But this is designed with the idea of settling up lands that are close to the railways and that have been passed over, I will admit frankly, for lands more desirable. The idea is to encourage people to go on those lands in order to thicken settlement under those conditions, to keep men working on the land and improving it until they get to the point where it will be self-supporting. I think there is a great necessity for assistance of this character wisely administered.
I have sought to recommend in this bill that we do not set up any elaborate establishment. In the western provinces we choose the Dominion lands agent in the particular district in which these lands are located, assisted by the
expert advice of our Soldier Settlement Board officials who have acquired a wide fund of information in regard to various localities in connection with the settlement of soldiers upon the land. These men will be a committee of three who will decide upon the character of the land upon which a loan is to be made and the standing of the settler, and they will protect the government in every way in connection with advancing money to these settlers. I have tried not to set up any elaborate machinery, but simply to create an organization that will assist the new-comer upon the land to a very reasonable degree in order to thicken settlement upon those crown lands that are available for settlement along the railway lines. #

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: What assistance, if any, will this Immigration bill grant to the settler coming into Canada who is willing to settle in the old provinces? maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
There is in the bill a special provision that will apply particularly to the Maritime provinces which have no crown lands, but the bill does not purport to touch other than crown lands in the other provinces of Canada. In British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec, if the provincial governments are in agreement, the same provision will apply to crown lands. As regards Ontario, I have in my hand a bill almost similar in character to the one I am describing this afternoon whereby that province lends money up to $500. I have not the Quebec bill under my hand, but in it there is a provision, almost similar in character, under which loans are made in connection with settlement in the new land in the northern district along the Grand Trunk Pacific. I am not aware that in British Columbia they have loan provisions of this kind, but they have in the two older provinces. This bill, however, does not purport to touch the class of farms that my hon. friend has just mentioned; it deals only with lands owned and held by the crown whether federally or provincially. As regards provincial crown lands exactly the same provisions will prevail with
Advances to Settlers

the single exception that the provincial officer in the latter case will be a member of the board. That is, the officer in charge of provincial crown lands will be substituted1 for the officer in charge of Dominion crown lands. The Soldier Settlement Board officials will perform the same service in the provinces and of course this will be done only by consent of the provinces if they wish to take advantage of the provisions of the bill.

speechtext:
I understood the minister to
say that these regulations would apply only to crown lands. Now I see that under section 8 of the resolution if a provincial government has not any crown lands it has the right to purchase suitable land for settlement. Will the minister explain *his apparent contradiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I was just
coming to that provision. It was designed primarily to meet the situation in the Maritime provinces. There I am told they have no crown lands available for settlement. In order to make the bill general in character and to avoid discrimination against any provinces without crown lands that wished to avail itself of the provisions of the bill, we have provided that under such circumstances a province may purchase suitable agricultural lands, and we will grant a certain amount of assistance, although it is true that this assistance is so meagre that it is hardly worth mentioning. If the provincial government wishes to put land into the hands of a new settler, we are prepared to make the necessary advance, of course always reserving priority of claim for repayment of our loan.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Why is not this left to the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: It will be; but in all probability some of the provinces will not care to take advantage of this measure.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: But they will have to pay for it just the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Not necessarily.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
If one province does
not participate, and two or three others do, would not the whole obligation be on the Dominion?
Mr. 'STEWART (Edmonton): Only to the extent of the losses. I think after all my hon. friend will agree that land settlement is so important a factor that any small loss which might accrue would not seriously affect any province whether it participated or not.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
That would depend on
the amount of the losses.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Might I ask-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: I would suggest to members on both sides of the House that they withhold their questions until the resolution is in committee. I am quite aware that the questions are very pertinent and very important, but in committee stage both on the resolution and on the bill hon. members will have ample opportunity to put their questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have almost concluded my remarks. I commend the resolution to the consideration of the House, for I think it will be of material assistance in settling lands that hitherto have not been made use of, and will thus consolidate settlement. Lest some member should object that there is plenty of good agricultural land awaiting settlement, I think I am safe in saying that it is scarcely the business of the federal government to undertake the settlement of such lands: but we did feel that some concession should be made to the Maritime provinces, whose governments are taking a very active interest in immigration and have signed agreements with us for the care and placement of the young boys that are being brought out from the Old Country. This is all to the good, for in all matters of immigration I should like to have the closest co-operation with the provincial governments through their local officials rather than attempt to do work by establishing federal officials in the various provinces. I think our efforts should be devoted largely to bringing out the right class of settlers and placing them in the hands of the provincial authorities, who, being conversant with the local situation, know where to place the newcomers to the best advantage and can give them sound advice. I am speaking now purely and simply of immigration for the settlement of our agricultural lands. We are bending all our energies to getting that class of settler, believing that later on there will be an opportunity for immigrants of the artisan class, although they are already coming in in fairly large numbers. This measure is designed solely for the purpose of advancing the necessary funds to help the settler to improve his holding until the day that it shall become self-supporting. I have no doubt a good deal of criticism can be offered against 'the proposal, but I do think it will materially help in settling lands that up to date have not been considered first-class for homesteading.

Advances, to Settlers

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no
objection to this resolution going through committee. I really want to give the minister credit for the best of intentions in introducing it, but he will have to forgive me if I cannot get enthusiastic over this venture. It is one of those measures which are very likely to be fairly popular at the initiation stage, but which leave a long train of sad memories in their wake. Not only so, but after they are immediately in operation there is an evidence of good results-often an illusory evidence. The very expenditure of considerable sums of government money produces a certain exhilaration and things look fine, but after the night of intoxication there is usually an awakening of bitterness; and I fancy we are going to suffer such experience in relation to this bill.
I must admit, first of all, that my doubts are very much related to the experience of the country with respect to soldier settlement. As respects soldier settlement, the minister throughout his entire term of office has been exceedingly fair to the whole scheme; he has given it, I think, a fair trial under his administration. He will admit with me, that if it was possible to launch such a scheme on sound lines, to barricade it against the rapacious and protect the treasury, these precautions were all taken.. But while all this is admitted we have to confess that first of all we did not succeed in preventing the inroads of the unscrupulous and the fraudulent. We can point to cases where, notwithstanding all our precautions, the fact that it was a government venture rendered it vulnerable, and at different points in the country we were imposed on right and left. This however was not the worst result. As time went on the unexpected developed, so that we find ourselves to-day under the necessity of entering upon a great new scheme of revaluation, a scheme which, on whatever principle in the world you put it, is bound to land the country in millions, yes, tens of millions of a loss. I know that is due practically altogether, or very largely, to the trend of land stock values in these later years. But to all the incidents to which the soldier settlement scheme was subject, to all the vicissitudes that harassed it, this new venture will also be exposed. It is going to be so exposed from day to day.
The minister says this is intended to help the settlement of rejected lands, those which have been passed up by the homesteaders. Well, perhaps it will for a time. But lands which the homesteader passed by when he
could get them free, when all he had to do was to live on them for a time each year for three years, lands which under those conditions are shunned will not be settled to any great extent by artificial means. Are we going to be further ahead in three, five, ten years? Our money will be there, but the homesteader will be gone, mainly for the reason that land which is not now settled along railway lines is in the main not worth settling. I do not believe that you will get a successful settlement upon such land by holding out the golden coin as an inducement to men to take up homesteads.
We are told that we have to do this because the provinces will not undertake the work, and that it is necessary in order to stimulate immigration. We all want to stimulate immigration; everyone knows that we need to. inaeea, it nas oeen stimulated pretty nearly to death ever since this government came into power. They started out with an immigration of 145,000, and it is now 85,000; and last year was the worst in many a long day. But are you going to stimulate immigration by offering rewards? I do not think that any country has ever yet found any similar scheme an incentive to permanent and successful immigration. I am not aware of any means of stimulating immigration except to provide work for the immigrant. The minister says that the only people whom the boards of trade want are men who will go on the land. It is a funny thing to me that everyone on earth wants to keep out competition except the farmer. We are all ready to give him all the competition possible and to give it to him at his own expense. Now, if I were a farmer I would want competition among people to whom I could sell my produce.	And as I am a farmer that is what I
want.	The best way to get immigration is
to bring about healthful industrial conditions. We will get that way immigration for the land just as well as for the town, and artificial stimulants are not going to conduce to anything like wholesome, continuous immigration.
The minister refers to the provinces. He says, "Well, it is true that we cannot be fair among them, because some of them have not crown lands and we cannot help those that have not. But in any case they will not lose anything except, perhaps, to the extent of bearing a share of the loss, which will be trifling." Are we sure that it will be trifling? The loss will be trifling if we go into the venture on a trifling scale; but if we undertake it on any substantial scale the loss will not be slight. I ask the minister to cast his

speechtext: I must disagree with my hon. friend. He has referred to the soldier settlement scheme, with the dissatisfaction and the losses that have accrued to it. I am bound to say that if the loans to the soldier settlers had been confined within more reasonable bounds the losses would not have been so great.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
More reasonable bounds
in what way ?

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
They were
given loans up to $7,000 at the start, and that is not being done to-day. The large percentage of the loss is due to the fact that we loaned far too much money. I believe that if any man in western Canada who had a reasonably decent homestead, not even a first class one, had been loaned $500 at that time, either he would have repaid it or the land today would be worth the money.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
The minister knows that abandoned homesteads in western Canada are legion, and so far as those which are not abandoned are concerned the men who were originally on them are very often not there to-day. Very few of them are. The minister says that we lost on soldier settlement because we loaned too much money. Well, we loaned only sufficient to get the men on the land. We had to lend too much for the simple reason that it took too much to get the land and stock. Now we are going to settle rejected homesteads, and homesteads on crown lands in those provinces where there are such lands, but the minister cannot put the scheme on a basis which will be fair among the provinces. I do not want to arouse sectional prejudice at all, but it does seem to me that it is absurd for the minister to contend that this is possible. There is no way of doing it. Take Ontario, for example: that province to-day has a scheme for advancing money for these very purposes, and they can supervise the whole thing much more easily than we can. The land is theirs and they can take care of it. And they too, I venture to say, will have a loss. Quebec has a corresponding scheme. Nova Scotia has not, because it has no crown lands, nor has New Brunswick. Now to the losses that will accrue in respect of those provinces

which have, these others will have to contribute, and there is no way of compensating them. The minister in the second last clause of the resolution has a scheme whereby he can give to Nova Scotia, or New Brunswick a half interest for two years on the purchase price of lands. He rightly describes this as meagre, I think he said trivial. Well, it is trivial.	It does not hold out the
slightest inducement, for not a province will buy on that basis. Imagine a province buying a piece of land privately owned, paying its value, and then turning it over to a settler. The settler borrows from this government and this government takes a first mortgage, giving the province a second mortgage for the purchase price of the land, and the inducement that gets the provinces to do thus is that the minister offers them the interest for one year. It is laughable. Never would a province venture upon the plan on such a basis. Therefore, you do expose those provinces which cannot come into the scheme to the necessity of subscribing towards it, bearing their share of the loan, in the first place, of the administration, in the second place, and of the ultimate loss, in the third. I warn the minister there will be a large cost of administration of this plan. I do not think he has devised it on a political basis, and I do not know that I can suggest at the moment anything very radical in the method of recommendation of the lands and of the loans, but I warn him that the cost of administration proportionate to the results will be very, very large. He will have to have a system of inspection, not only of the farms, in the first place, but of the farming, in the second place: he will have to have a system of supervision; he will have to have a staff here of a very considerable number to conduct all the correspondence with the municipalities and the like, and as the whole scheme develops, the top will increase in weight even after the base commences to diminish.

How do you get rid of them here? In the one case you can buy

The difference is this: In the one case the man knows he owes the money to a private owner, and knows he has to make good; in the other case, he owes the money to the government, and does not feel he has to make good.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Long experience has taught us that it is correct. It may be-I do not know-that there are certain obligations the minister has entered into in good faith which make this scheme necessary as a complement to his immigration policy. If such is the case, it would be some measure of justification, but with the tremendous load which is on our backs now and which is to become greater and greater if this other resolution regarding the revaluation of soldier lands goes through, as well as others, with all these obligations I fancy that we are hardly doing justice to the general interests of this country to place upon the shoulders of the taxpayer still another burden.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: In making comparison between this scheme and the soldier settlement scheme, the leader of the opposition touched very lightly on one great difference. It is a difference which I think should receive a great deal of consideration at the present time. At the time the land and equipment was purchased for the soldiers going on the land, prices were at the peak. I will give just one instance. A farm that I know quite well for which the purchaser refused 860 per acre, was sold in two or three years afterwards on very, very easy terms at $29 per acre. In those years when the soldiers were going on the land the prices for land and equipment were at the peak, but the prices obtainable for the products of the farm, for the wheat, the oats, the cattle and everything the soldier produced were low. The peak prices were the prices he had to pay for his land and his stock. I think it is no exaggeration to say that horses which were purchased for the soldiers at a price of say, $200, in the course of three or four years' time were worth not more than $50. I do not give those as the exact prices, but that is about the proportion. In a conversation I had with the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) a few nights ago, I pointed to one settlement where some fifty-two farms were taken up and appraised by a very efficient appraiser, a mutual friend, and I believe that of the fifty-two, fifty-one suc-
