speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
ceeded under the very adverse conditions I have mentioned-buying land, stock and equipment at peak prices and receiving for the products of the farm low prices. The prices of the chattels purchased had dropped 50 per cent in many cases. An hon. member behind me says 150 per cent. At all events they have dropped 50 per cent and more in some cases.
I believe the greatest danger to this scheme lies in the appraising of the land. Some very peculiar things took place under the soldier settlement scheme. I am not sure that all of them ever came to the attention of the board, but I know of one that worked out like this. A piece of land that was nothing but a sand bank, not worth in my estimation more than $10 an acre at the most, and I would call that price high, was appraised at $30 an acre and sold at that price. But that was not all. The owner of that land, I believe -I have not positive proof, but I have sufficient to cause me to believe it is an actual fact-made a quiet bargain with the three returned men who were going to take three quarters of the section, that if they could persuade the board to purchase at $30 an acre he would make them a gift of the other quarter. The deal went through. However, the three returned men found out although they got the quarter for nothing, that having purchased the three quarters at $30 an acre after the deflation took place, they had made a very bad deal indeed. I have not the slightest hesitation in believing that the gentleman who made the appraisement of those lands was not absolutely honest. I cannot think that any man who possessed the experience the man in question is said to have had honestly appraised that land at $30 per acre. In discussing this matter with certain officials they advanced the excuse that the scheme at that time was an entirely new one, that they had to pick out new men, that they were up against a difficulty and in some cases secured men highly recommended only to discover that they were very poor appraisers. As the minister has pointed out, there is machinery that will be available under the new scheme, and I have no doubt that those responsible for its operation will profit from the mistakes made in the past.
Another point to which I wish to allude before taking my seat is this. The right hon. leader of the opposition stated that he believed that homesteads that have been passed over are hardly worth taking up, and that it is just a question whether it would be wise to insist upon settlement going on to these homesteads. If it were a case of the open prairie
IMr. Millar.]
that statement might be true, but some of the lands on which it is proposed to settle these newcomers are potentially valuable. Where the land is good it will make excellent and valuable farms. In the case of lands covered with scrub sometimes the timber will be large enough to possess some commercial value but for the most part it is useless. Once that timber is removed, however, the lands will be found to be valuable. I am inclined to think that if the appraisement is surrounded with proper safeguards the present scheme will have undoubted value in connection with the settling of some of these lands.
Mr. MEiIGHEN:	How are you going to
appraise lands that nobody will take now for nothing? Is not that the very land that is to be used?

I think it may be easily
understood that land that many settlers might not take now for nothing, especially when they have to clear it without assistance, would be acceptable to them if they were going to receive an advance of money to enable them to make, a start, lit is true the amount is not very large but it is an encouragement to them to take the land and improve it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That may be. They may take the land and may get money to help them to carry on, but that does not affect the question of the appraisement of the land as it stands. How can you appraise land that nobody will take as it stands?

I
should not like the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition in regard to the Manitoba farm loan scheme to pass without a comment or two. I do not think the right hon. gentleman wants to do an injury to any organization; I think he has confused the farm loan scheme with that of rural credits. There is no doubt that the rural credit societies of Manitoba have experienced losses but the loans in such cases were made on the operations of the farmer. The scheme of farm loans in Manitoba has been a success. It has not only proved profitable but it has been successful in keeping down the rate of interest. In the case of these loans the Manitoba farmer is getting money at the rate of 7 per cent, plus 1 per cent for amortization extending over a period of 30 years. This means an interest rate of 8 per cent. On the other hand you will find a great many farmers to-day paying a rate of interest as high as 8J and 8|, and in some cases 9 per cent, not only in Manitoba but in the provinces farther west. So that I think that the farm loan scheme in

Advances to Settlers
Manitoba even if it has not made large profits has certainly helped the situation as far as loans on farm lands are concerned.
I do not know how the scheme before the committee will work out, but I have this in mind; in a good many parts of western Canada-and for this I think the lack of proper colonization schemes is to blame-we have allowed a settler to locate here, and another there, and so on; they are scattered over quite a lot of territory. Then we have crown land adjacent to the settlers that are there to-day. But their numbers are too small to support schools, to build roads, and to carry out other improvements. If the present scheme can be properly worked out the settlers in question, few in number and virtually exiled, will receive a considerable augmentation of settlement and it will be possible to creat a community life which is largely absent to-day. If the scheme has this result it will be a good thing.
Another point to which I wish to allude is that this is the first time to my knowledge that we have given Canadian citizens a certain benefit under our immigration policy. We know of lots of men who have left the farm because of circumstances over which they had no control. They are at present in the city engaged in a desperate effort to make both ends meet. Now. if we could settle these people upon crown lands and advance them a sum of money to help them to carry out certain improvements they might be induced to return to the land and establish homes for themselves which would be a decided benefit to Canada. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) asked the question " Why not give those in all other walks of life the same advantages?" As a matter of fact we know that if the agricultural industry in Canada is prosperous all other industries will prosper likewise. Agriculture is a primary industry and everybody knows that if we have a prosperous agricultural community the rest of Canada is prosperous also. Suppose one had entered a manufacturing establishment two or three years ago, and had asked the manager why depression existed, his answer, if he were not intoxicated with the principle of protection, would be that it was due to the lack of purchasing power on the part of the Canadian people. He would say that was the reason why our industries were not prosperous. I have asked that question of dozens and dozens of manufacturers in the province of Ontario and they too gave me the same answer. While settlement was going on in western Canada, while the construction of railroads was in 14011-120)
progress, and immigrants were coming in great volume to this country, we never heard the manufacturer complain about the lack of business. But depression came and hit the agriculturist first. Then, two or three years afterwards, the manufacturer began to feel the pinch. This experience may do our manufacturers a lot of good and render them more efficient.

I desire to occupy the attention of the committee for a moment or two on this question. I am opposed to the principle of the resolution because I am opposed to parliament eternally spoon-feeding the people.
I do not think we can ever develop a self-respecting and1 self-reliant race as long as we continue to follow methods of this kind. Neither do I think that in this good Dominion of Canada such a scheme is necessary.
I remember reading a debate in this House some time ago when the then member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) said! that he knew a gentleman, presumably himself, who came to this country as a stowaway or something of that character. He had grown, if not immensely wealthy, at least very well off, and ended up by being a representative of the people in this parliament. That is the class of people we want in Canada, self-reliant people who can make good if given the opportunity, and1 I might say that he is no exception. There are hundreds and thousands and tens of thousands of such people in the country. Neither do I think that this proposition is a fair one to the dominion or to the province. As my right hon. leader has pointed out, you cannot make it fair to the provinces. I do not think it is going to be fair to the settler. I think you could not put a settler under a greater handicap than to put him where he could not grow a first-class crop. Of necessity his income and earning power is going to be greatly reduced from the fact that he is on inferior land. Why then should this country go into a proposition of this kind, loan money on our own property, or give away property which is inferior and ask a man to go on it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
May I
correct my hon. friend. He seems to be under the impression that the loans will be made on inferior land. That is not the proposition at all. A great deal of this land now under timber and brush is first-class agricultural land, the very best land we have in western Canada. I speak with some knowledge. I am sure when my hon. friend goes
Advances to Settlers

into northern Ontario he will have the same thing to say about the clay belt there. There is no better land than the olay belt in that district. Of course it is considerably to the north, but bear in mind the trouble is not the quality of the land, it is the difficulty in acquiring 'the land, to get it under cultivation.
I was taking the minister's own word. He gave me to understand this was inferior land that had been passed over when settlers were going there.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On account of the brush.

On account of the
difficulty in clearing. I think it would be of infinitely more importance to Canada if this government would get busy and so shape its policy that the people of the country could get something to do, and get some money for doing the work rather than simply loaning money on propositions which they admit are fraught with great difficulty and loss. The proposition is unsound and1 unfair from the dominion standpoint, from the provincial standpoint, and unfair from the standpoint of the settler. I want to voice my objection again to the eternal propositions coming before this House and country for the spoon-feeding of the people. We wili never get into this country good self-reliant people so long as they have to rely on the government to be spoon-fed. This class of people will never make a living.

Would the hon. member
apply that to manufacturing as well?

I desire to tell the hon. gentleman and this House-and I have stated it in parliament before-that there is no more justification for giving assistance to men going on the land than there is for giving assistance to men who are going into a manufacturing industry, and when we are going into .propositions of this kind we are showing favours to different classes of people in the country, which we have not the right to do.

I
see very little difference between giving a bonus to a man going on the land and giving a bonus to a manufacturer by protection, the latter being spoon-fed to the limit. I heartily endorse what the minister said with regard to the necessity of consolidating settlement, but I do not entirely agree with his plan for crary-ing it out. I think one of our troubles in western Canada has been caused by spreading settle-

ment out too much. We surveyed land far beyond the reach of the ordinary settler. The moment land is surveyed and thrown open for settlement, it is a direct invitation for people to go in and occupy it. The settler is in a postion, after he has located on land a long way from the railway, to demand of ' the government railway facilities, and the government is under a moral obligation to provide him with those facilities when he goes in there, after the land has been thrown open for settlement. If we survey land too far out for settlement, men go in there and locate, start to build homes, clear up the brush, drain sloughs, organize municipalities, a large amount of money is spent on roads, schools 'being necessary, debentures are issued-against what? The most of the land is unpatented. After a few years, in many of the frontier settlements, a great number of these people, I think oh an average in the bush districts probably SO per cent of them, move out. You see the position in which that leaves the other 50 per cent. Their taxation is automatically doubled. There is continual pressure brought to bear on the provincial authorities-and I think the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Railways will bear me out in this-for improvement and for roads. The municipalities are burdened with the same thing, and instead of settling a problem you have created a new one. To my mind that is just what this legislation is going to do. It is not going to settle the problem that the minister has in mind, but he will create a new problem. I think I can speak with authority on this matter, because in my constituency we have about one hundred and twenty-five miles of a frontier on the bush land. There were large settlements there, but hundreds of these settlers have left and given up their farms. I am safe in saying that there are scores of homesteads which after being proved up, have reverted to the municipalities for taxes. Those homesteads have been improved and men have spent the best part of their lives there. Money has been spent on roads and money has been spent for schools, and in one district I know there are two schools idle to-day, not being used, but the debentures are still held against the land'. The settlers are still striving to make a living. When you go out to the frontier settlement, between the old settlement and the railway, you pass miles and miles of good agricultural land not occupied and some of that is partly improved. My 'hon. friend asks, why? There are various reasons why. Agriculture out there has not been prosperous. Farmers have been evicted. Their mortgages have been foreclosed. Others

Advances to Settlers
have gone voluntarily. Conditions are improving now, no doubt about that. In other cases, farmers bought more land than they could handle. When they found they could not handle it they had to give up some of it. I say to the minister that if he wants to accomplish the object he has in view 'he should endeavour to consolidate our settlement and converge on the existing settlements where educational, transportation and other facilities are already provided. In that way he might accomplish something. He could use money to assist settlement on lands privately owned. He may say that that is a provincial issue. I say that it is not a provincial issue entirely. Colonization is a federal issue and not a provincial issue. As the hon. leader of the opposition has said, these lands are available for purchase to-day at very low price?, lower than we have seen in western Canada for many years. The conditions out there are improving to a considerable extent. J believe that if many of these men could get assistance to locate on this class of land to-day they could make good.
Instead of opening up new lands where we have to build new roads, new schools, and to provide all the municipal machinery and so put further burdens on provincial and dominion authorities, let us use the facilities that we have. One of the problems of our railways and of our private business to-day is the overhead. Any business man knows that if he can double, triple or quadruple his turnover, he can reduce his overhead. By thickening up our settlement, by filling up those lands privately owned which are adjacent to our present transportation facilities, we can as a nation substantially reduce our overhead. We do not need to go outside of this country to get many desirable settlers for this class of land. The minister has referred to the "back to the land" movement from the cities. I know I can go to small towns in western Canada and to our cities in the east and in the west and I can get thousands of men, many of whom have had considerable agricultural experience, to go out on the land. They will not go fifteen or twenty miles into the bush; they are too shrewd to go there; but if you give them a little assistance to buy good privately owned land adjacent to the towns, they will go there and tens of thousands of them can make good.
That will help to solve the problem of unemployment which at present exists in the cities. It will assist us in our taxation problems in the country, and that is a terrible problem in some of our districts where many
men have been thrown out of or have abandoned their farms. It will assist in solving another problem. As I have said, one of our problems is that many of our farmers have too much land, perhaps on account of being over-speculative at a particular period when the government at Ottawa as well as private business concerns were demanding greater production. The farmer was pleaded with and preached at to produce, and produce, and produce. That was the proper thing to do at the time and there was a time when it was a profitable thing to do because, during the latter ye^rs of the war and indeed two years after the war, mass production was the proper kind of. production for the farmer. He could use engines instead of horses and in that way cultivate a large area much more cheaply than a small one. But those conditions do not obtain to-dav. The ^rice of engine fuel is just as high now as it was then. The price of horse feed has gone away down; it is not more than perhaps 25 to 30 per cent of what it was in the years to which I refer, and the farmer finds now that he must go-back to the use of horses almost exclusively in the cultivation of his land. That means; that he cannot cultivate on a large scale; that he must get down to a matter of more intensive cultivation. Many of those farmers who purchased more land than they could handle are in a position where they are liable to lose everything they possess. A man may have a joint mortgage against his land, whether it is a section or two sections as the case may be. If he can sell two or three quarter sections to new settlers under some scheme, the government might very well take hold of it. This would take a tremendous burden off his shoulders, thicken up settlement, bring in more men to pay taxes and help to clear bush on this class of land because there will probably be only sixty, seventy or eighty acres cleared on a quarter section. It will be better to get settlers on such land who will clear the balance of the quarter sections, rather than to send men out fifteen, twenty, twenty-five miles into the bush to clear new land away from settlement altogether.
At one place in my constituency we have what was at one time a very large settlement, forty miles from a railway. The men there were brought in by the Soldier Settlement Board. The land is the finest class of land you will find in western Canada, an ideal place, but there is no railway and the inevitable has happened. Some of these men have cleared up as much as 100 acres on a quarter and after doing so have walked out and left it. We do not want any more of that and
Advances to Settlers

I would earnestly plead with the minister to use the same legislation, because it has some merits, but in a different way. If you assist a man to be relocated on privately owned land, you have the same opporunity to get first security on it as you have in connection with your homestead fifteen, eighteen or twenty miles from a railway on the edge of a forest reserve. Where is your security in connection with that? The farmer who owns the land-or whether it is a speculator or business man or bank or mortgage company it makes no difference-in many cases would permit the government to * take a first mortgage and put his own equity on as a second mortgage. It would be of considerable assistance to the settler to have a first mortgage of SI,000, let us say, at a low rate of interest and spread over a long period of years, and many men under some such plan as that could be induced to go on the land whereas under this plan those who went on the land would be almost sure to fail.

How would the hon.
member give the federal government priority over everybody else on privately owned land?

Supposing these is a
mortgage of 13,000 against a quarter section of land and a settler wants to buy it. The man who has the $3,000 mortgage would be only too glad to accept the $1,000 as a cash payment, give the federal government security for that, and take a second mortgage for the 12,000.
And give the government priority?
Yes.

Mr. Speaker, post-mortems are not valuable except in so far as we gather therefrom some knowledge that is useful at the present or in the future. I am not very much concerned about our experience in connection with soldier settlement, for instance, or the advances we made to farmers who were in the drouth-stricken areas of Alberta, or other advances, except in so far as they induce me to believe that no government assistance as such has thus far been successful in western Canada. I regret to say that in Manitoba to which the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) referred a moment ago, I think he will find that not only did the government lose money on the rural credits, but they also lost money, as reported by their own officers, in advances they made on farm lands as such. In Saskatchewan, where the administration was in the hands of an old loan company 
officer, their experience has been very much more satisfactory. Even in the land banks of the United States that have been in existence only a short time, there have been substantial losses during the last few years, and recently the government imposed upon those banks the necessity of setting up a reserve with respect to all property which they now hold under foreclosure.
The question that we are considering is whether or not this country shall put into unpatented or undeeded property $5,000,000 per annum at a rate of interest of 5 per cent per annum, repayable in ten years, the first payment to commence at the expiration of the second year. To that question baldly put in that way, I should think the answer should be in the negative. If on the other hand you surround the proposal with sufficient safeguards, there are a number of deserving cases that come to the attention of most of us every week of our lives, either by correspondence or by personal interview, that warrant the government in doing something to intensify settlement that is so sparse especially in western Canada. I wholly agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Air. Campbell) as to the causes that have brought about present conditions in western Canada. Nothing struck me more in the early days than to observe people going far away from a railway and settling and then the clamour that commenced for railways. In addition to the factors that have been mentioned as bringing about the condition referred to, there is one other factor which I think the minister might well bear in mind, that is, that lands have been stricken by drouth. Areas were opened for settlement that should never have been homesteaded. Especially is that so in Alberta and in one comer of Saskatchewan.
Now, the Minister of the Interior has observed that there are six million acres of land in Alberta within fifteen miles of railways and available for homesteading. But as I read the agreement that is now before the House, those lands are to be transferred to the provincial government, in whom the title would then be vested. These lands have not been homesteaded, and the reasons are twofold. First, in the northern part of the province there is considerable timber and railways have been extended north and west by the Dunvegan line, north by the Waterways railway, and to Athabasca Landing by the Canadian National. Still those homesteads have not been settled within fifteen miles of the railways for the simple and obvious reason that no person desired to take up the land.

Advances to Settlers
There has been homesteading in the Peace river territory, and we have had demands for railways from men who have settled in those remote sections. In the southern part of the province there are still some homesteads left, and there is still a considerable area in the central part of the province, but no one has attempted to homestead on those lands for the last twenty-five years. Only yesterday I received a communication with respect to a quarter section once homesteaded, and the reports are that no man can possibly go upon it and make even a pretence towards a living.
Under these circumstances is it fair or just or right that we should pledge the public credit with the hope that we will ever get back the money that we lend to the people who go upon those lands that for twenty-five years have been passed by by those who might have occupied them on payment of $15. Although patents to the land cannot be obtained in less than five years, we are told that we may be able to get back the money in eight years, commencing at the expiration of two years, with interest at 5 per cent per annum. Can we hope that at the end of the second year the homesteader may be able to pay interest on $1,000, that is, $50, plus one-eighth of the principal, which is $125. But in my judgment, having regard to what I have observed in the operation of loans of that character in that part of Canada, this would be nothing more nor less than an admission of failure before we commenced.
Now, it is said there are millions of acres of land available in Saskatchewan. I am perfectly certain that the ministers from Saskatchewan will bear me out that any land available for homesteading within fifteen miles of a railway in Saskatchewan does not belong to the class of land on which we expect people to make successful settlement. In Manitoba there are three million acres of vacant land. Why? Because you have the Hudson Bay railway extending into the northern part of that province, and the lands within fifteen miles of it have not been settled because they are not of the character that attracts settlers for any purpose other than ranching.
Then why should we do this at all? I think there are some reasons why we should. I have observed a very considerable number of people during my residence in western Canada who have the merit of a willingness to work-which is not common in some parts of Canada-and yet despite all they may do they have not been able to get even $500 of additional capital to enable them to start
upon the pathway of success. Those people I think this country might well assist. I do not agree with my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) when he says we may rely upon the grim determination and the hardihood of settlers in these days to make homes for themselves in the wilderness, to succeed by their own unaided efforts or perish. Before the war that was true, but since settlement conditions have entirely changed, and we can no longer expect to attract people to this country and get them settled successfully under the same conditions as obtained before the war. With respect to that I am perfectly certain. The great success, if it was a success-I have my opinion as to that, but this is not the time or place to discuss it-with respect to settlement in western Canada was during those days when we were spending borrowed money on railways and paying interest on the borrowed money out of the money so borrowed, with the result that this country to-day is called upon to pay $30,000,000 per annum or even more for that costly experiment we engaged in at that time. Now my friend the minister knows, because he is aware of the conditions, that the very best settlement from the standpoint of getting results was settlement created at the time when men were able to find employment at certain periods of tihe year and then go up on their homesteads and utilize the money they had earned. What the country is demanding to-day is an opportunity for men to work; that is my observation; and if we can supply work of any kind for those who come into the Dominion, then advances of $500 or $1,000 would be absolutely secure; but if we merely intend to put people upon land within fifteen miles of a railway that has not been homesteaded for the last twenty-five years, and tell them as soon as they have a barbed wire fence around it and have put up a log or a sod hut they can come and get $500 or $1,000, that money is irretrievably and inevitably lost. I am satisfied of that. But if we can create conditions in this country, as I think we can if we only desire so to do, by which there would be some employment afforded to those who come here, especially having regard to the seasonal conditions that prevail, then those who have shown their desire to have a permanent stake in the country and have indicated by their earnings or savings to the extent I have mentioned that they desire to settle on land passed up by others, this country would be warranted in making some advances to them.
I fear very much that the minister will be not only disappointed with the working out
Advances to Settlers

of this proposal, but I think it will afford one more reason for a raid being made upon the government. To that extent I agree with my friend from Muskoka, that every time we weaken the fibre of our people by inducing them to believe that the government must take the place that has been occupied in times past by the hardy manhood of the people themselves, to that extent we have done injury to the country. But if we assist where there is ambition, if we aid where there is aspiration, then we have done some good to the community.
Now, this resolution does not say that lands must be within fifteen miles of a railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh yes.
I am told by those who have had to do with the handling of farn^ products that even fifteen miles in these days is too great a distance.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the limit.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: :I may tell my hon. friend that 190 homesteads were taken up in western Saskatchewan last year in the wooded areas.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And they have been passed by for twenty-five years. Across the Saskatchewan river, within fifteen miles of the Grand Trunk Pacific, there is another splendid area of first-class land, which has never been taken up.

What the minister says
is absolutely true. There is no doubt that wherever men have to spend from three to ten dollars an acre to clear land to make it available for the profitable production of crops, such land will always be avoided, the preference being given to prairie lands. What the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Mc-Gibbon) has said is quite correct. In the early days of settlement in eastern Canada the people of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Quebec had to hew their homes out of the wilderness. But that is entirely a different thing from establishing homes on the prairies. There has been no disposition on the part of the prairie settler to take up land where he has had to do any clearing, even of scrub and brush, to any considerable extent. No great settlement of homestead lands has been passed up in southern Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
think so.

As I have already said,
I fear the minister is destined to be greatly disappointed by a scheme such as is proposed. I have an idea that what has happened in the past will happen again. A desperate effort is always made by the political organizer to induce people to undertake things of this kind. The organizer will tell them, ''Here is your chance. If j'ou only do certain things, you are bound to secure the desired results." My hon. friend knows this; he has had as much experience of it as I have had. And this is not confined to one party. We know that during the days of the distribution of the drought relief such incidents were not uncommon. I would advise the minister to reduce the amount and to make the experiment for one year only, trying under those conditions to induce.people to take up settlements in the vicinity of districts already settled, rather than going far afield and afterwards
making demands for telephones, schools, rural mail delivery, better roads and, lastly, increased transportation facilities in the way of railroads.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Duff in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry? Carried.

I trust, Mr. Chairman, you
are not going to carry it so rapidly as this.
I wish to make no reflections, but I think the Speaker was rather hasty in calling "Carried" before.
There is one objection that I think may be made to this resolution, and -that is that while the amount is -large, $5,000,000 a year, it is also unlimited as to time. I do not think, under -the present condition of the finances of this country, that an experiment of this nature t-o the extent of $5,000,000 a year should be unlimited as to time.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I intended
to say in reply to the hon. member for West Calgary that I have no particular objection to a reduction of the amount. Indeed, we likely shall not be called on to spend any of t-he -money this year, but my hon. friend will readily understand that if settlement takes place under the provisions of the act, the persons who settle on the land and make improvements will expect to have advances made to them in the succeeding year, and that is one of the difficulties in limiting it to one year. I have no objection to limiting: it to three years, and, when the bill is introduced, to cutting down the figure to a very reasonable amount, if that will meet my hon. friend's objection.
Mr. -CAHAN:	Mr. -Chairman, it certainly
will go a long way toward meeting the objection I had in mind, if the amount can be reduced, and- if the term during which the experiment is to be carried on can be limited. As a matter of fact, the constituency which I represent, -and this applies I believe -to the whole of the eastern provinces, is desirous of going a very long way in order to assist, in the development of the western provinces, bu-t there -must be a limit to the liabilities-which the whole country w-ill undertake in the next few years in that respect. We have-this liability, and if it is not inopportune to say so, we have the -liability coming in connection with rural credits, which lis a somewhat similar -application of public funds. Then we have the pension proposal, which
Advances to Settlers

I understand will require about twenty to twenty-five million dollars a year, if it is to be carried out according to the terms proposed in the resolution. Then we have the liability to which I called attention the other day in connection with the West Indies, which may amount, if we carry out that engagement, to a capital outlay of some nine or ten million dollars, and an outlay to make up the deficiency in earnings running anywhere from $300,000 or $400,000 to $1,000,000 a year, depending on the extent to which the scheme is carried out.
We are in a very critical position in this country at the present time. Hon. gentlemen do not seem to realize the burden of debt and the burden of taxation which we are now carrying, and which, if you take your municipal, your provincial, and your federal taxation, all of which we have to bear, amounts to nearly one-quarter of the productive energies of this country. Further, while the east is prepared to make large concessions to the west, if you impose too large burdens upon the east, it must break; it cannot carry the burden that it is carrying. Since confederation was established in 1867 the east has willingly carried that burden, and it is carrying it to-day. In proportion to the wealth of those western provinces, Manitoba*, Alberta 'and 'Saskatchewan, -the individual wealth of the eastern provinces is far less, and the eastern -provinces are far less able to carry the burden than the west. The west is more prosperous to-day than any other part of this country, and I am thankful for it; -but if you burden -the east without giving, as I think, proper encouragement to the establishment of remunerative industry in the east, this country will break so far -as the east is concerned1; it will be impossible to carry the burden of debt and taxation which has [been already rolled- up. Without saying one word of disparagement of the west, the great burden of our taxation comes upon the eastern provinces, and they are carrying as -heavy -a burden as it is possible for men to carry under the present industrial conditions. I am thankful, therefore, -that the minister has saved me from talking half an hour by the very reasonable concessions which he says he is prepared to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend surely is not arguing that the individual in the east carries more taxation than the individual in the west?

The eastern individual
carries more than the western; there is absolutely no doubt about it. There is no doubt that the eastern provinces are carrying by taxation a large portion of the cost of shipping every ton of wheat that comes from the west to the east. That is according to the return which was brought down for my hon. friend from Muskoka, and to which he referred. It is not dealing with the present year-and I am not dealing with the present year, but in the two previous years this country as a whole paid a very considerable portion of the cost of transporting the wheat from the west to the east, and I think it is prepared to make large concessions in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That was
not the question I asked my hon. friend. I understood him to be arguing that the individual in the east was carrying more taxation than the individual in the west.
Mi-. CAHAN: I cannot discuss intelligently or compare our municipal taxation in the east with the municipal taxation in the west, because I have not the figures of municipal taxation. But so far as federal taxes are concerned there is absolutely no doubt, anyway you look at it, that the great bulk of the taxation of this country is being carried at a higher rate per capita in the eastern provinces than in any of the provinces of the middle west, and furthermore, it is being carried out of a per capita wealth much less in the east than in those provinces of the middle west. I am glad the amount involved in this proposal is to be decreased to a more reasonable limit. But consider the aggregate burden we are rolling up: We are also going to revalue the soldier settlement lands, a proposal which bids fair, if my information is at all Correct, to place a further burden of forty or fifty million dollars upon the whole country by the reduction of the amount of outstanding loans and the assumption of that reduction by the Dominion treasury and the east will have to bear a very considerable share of it. Then there is the rural credits scheme, the pension scheme, the proposals in connection with the Hudson bay, and all the rest. I say that unless you limit those obligations and at the same time give us an opportunity to increase our industrial efforts in the east you are placing a burden upon this country that, in my opinion, can have only one result. I have said before, and I wish to repeat it, I have no prejudice whatsoever against the west. I am anxious, and I believe

Advances to Settlers
the whole of the east is anxious, to assist in building up this country as a whole, whether it be the western provinces or the eastern provinces.

There is a provision in the proposed arrangement regarding the provinces which do not have crown lands suitable for the purpose of carrying out the desired object. The minister very correctly describes what is proposed as a very meagre provision, so meagre indeed that he thinks-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: May I correct my hon. friend? I am afraid that a different meaning from that intended has been given to a statement of mine. If the provinces have the lands and are desirous that the Dominion shall advance money to put settlers upon them, then the Dominion will advance the whole $1,000. The meagre provision 1 spoke of was the assistance granted the provinces to purchase the land.

There are some crown
lands in New Brunswick.

Some of the provinces
have crown lands not suitable for settlement, and in order to make this provision apply generally the minister recommends the provision set out in clause 8 of the resolution. He described that as a very meagre provision and I agree with him absolutely.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is towards the purchase of the land.

Towards the purchase
of the land, yes. I wish to remind the minister, and I have already pointed out the fact many times, that the attention of parliament is too strongly drawn and directed towards settlement in certain portions of the west, whereas other portions of the Dominion might, with great profit and even greater fairness, receive equal attention at the hands of the ministerial head of the Immigration department.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend's province is in a very superior position in the matter of fares for settlers because it takes very much less money to bring settlers to that province.
Mr. MacLAREtN: I understand the arrangement to which the minister refers has been agreed upon but has not yet been brought into effect. I should like the minister to point out to the committee anything in the nature of an advantage to the Maritimes in matters of this kind that has been carried out in the past few years. What we are dealing with
here is something which it is hoped to secure in the immediate future. I think my contention is correct that the immigration policy of the government has been too restricted in its outlook, and that there has been a failure to apply it equally to all portions of the Dominion. My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) pointed out the great difficulties that arise as a result of sparsity of settlement. In the remote portions of the country that difficulty would be encountered more easily than in the more settled parts of Canada. I would urge once more that settlement should proceed gradually from the populated districts outward rather than that it should be directed to remote and sparsely settled parts of Canada. At the present time I do not see that this proposal will apply to any extent to the eastern portion of the Dominion. I presume the minister will agree with that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I must confess that I am ignorant of the agricultural situation in the Maritime provinces, at all events I am not familiar with it. But my hope was that something might be accom-lished through the medium of this policy to settle the vacant lands of those provinces. I understand there are in the Maritime provinces a number of vecant and abandoned lands, although an abandoned farm has not a very pleasant sound to the ear of an incoming settler. That was a difficulty that was encountered in connection with the soldier settlement lands. At the same time I am informed that there are a large number of farms in the Maritime provinces of fairly good quality that are available for settlement to the newcomer. My hope was that perhaps the provinces might take up this problem in conjunction with the Dominion, in which case wp would make these loans to establish the newcomers.

I should like to ask the minister one question, because I can see how this proposal is likely to affect the province of Quebec to a very considerable extent. The minister has stated that the land coming under this scheme must be situated within fifteen miles of a railway. Such a provision, whether established by regulation or by statute, is going to militate extremely against the province of Quebec and will absolutely prevent the application of this scheme to districts in our province where settlement is needed, these districts being in some cases fifteen, twenty and, perhaps, twenty-five miles from the railway. I should therefore be very glad if the minister, when preparing the regulations which
Advances to Settlers

are to govern the matter, would take into consideration the fact that other parts of Canada as well as the west have to be kept in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am surprised to know that there is not a large quantity of land in the province of Quebec within fifteen miles of a railway.
All the crown lands that are being settled at the present time are situated more than fifteen miles from a railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend does not suggest that there are no crown lands unsettled within fifteen miles of the existing railways?
There is very little left in our part of the country within that distance.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I am in accord with the
spirit of this resolution. The minister states that he wishes to settle vacant lands throughout the Dominion. I do not, however, follow him in his argument that the present proposal is going to carry out that purpose. The first clause of the resolution provides that the minister may make loans to settlers on the basis of improvement of land and farm buildings erected, and the amount of such advance is to be $1,000 for a Canadian citizen and $500 for an outsider. In other words after the man has been induced to go on the land and has demonstrated to the government that he can support his family and make improvements he is entitled to receive aid which however he no longer requires. He has demonstrated that he can make a living and support his family. Then the government intimates that it is prepared to come to his assistance. I do not see the soundness of any such reasoning. It seems to me that if assistance is given it should be given in the first instance, because the type of settler that you are going to attract to these vacant lands is likely to be a man of very limited means. Now, if the intending settler has certain moneys of his own that will enable him to live for a period of two or three years, erect his buildings, and carry out desired improvements, he does not need to settle on vacant land. There are hundreds and thousands of acres of more or less improved land in western Canada today and which, if they can be purchased, will be taken in preference to vacant land. There are lands which can be purchased in western Canada to-day on the basis of a share of the crop payment without the purchaser putting up one dollar of his own money. And upon

these lands buildings have been erected in many cases. Buildings have already been erected on these lands, therefore I say this proposal does not encourage settlement on vacant lands. If we are to encourage settlement' on vacant lands the assistance should come at the beginning of the term, not after the man has demonstrated that he is capable of making a living there. I am opposed to any resolution providing for making a direct loan to the people from any government of this country. It has been proven a failure, especially in my own province of Manitoba, under the rural credit scheme. It has been a curse rather than a blessing to the people of that province, and I think every member from western Canada will bear me out in that statement. The government in Manitoba is facing a loss at least of $500,000 under that scheme.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Yes. Those loans were
made, I might say, to farmers already established upon the land with the object of improving their buildings and stock and making the business a success. If that policy was a failure under those conditions, where the farmers were already established on the land, how can hon. gentlemen expect inexperienced men taking up vacant land to make a success of it and be able to repay the money to the government? The principle of the government lending money directly to the people is to my mind absolutely wrong. We know that this is merely a sop and does not deal with the question in a big way. You have your other immigration schemes as well. Clause 8 states that if a provincial government, not having suitable crown lands available, acquires by purchase suitable land for settlement under the provisions of this legislation, the minister may pay to the provincial government a sum not exceeding one-half of the interest on the purchase price of such lands. If that provision was carried out you would add to the difficulties under which the municipalities are suffering to-day. You purchase the lands from private interests, and they become crown lands. Those lands are now taxable, and if those settlers leave them they revert to the crown, and any taxes that are paid on them at the present time will not be payable in future to the municipality.
Those are my main objections to this resolution. I believe the same result would be achieved by the government making a survey of all the different areas throughout the west, in co-operation with existing institutions such as agricultural societies, boards of trade, and the different locals of the United Farmers of

Advances to Settlers
the west, so that information would be at hand in concise form respecting lands which are available at the present time for settlement. There are many pieces of land in the well settled districts which the owners would be only too pleased to let go to men who wanted to settle on the land. If a man living in any of the cities of Canada to-day wishes to go on the land there is absolutely nothing to prevent him. Many farmers in the central provinces would only be too glad to get men and families to assist them, because many of them have too much land and not enough help to cultivate it. Some of these lands are capable of producing from 33 1-3 to 50 per cent more than they are producing at the present time with limited labour. Intending settlers from any of the cities of Canada, or incoming immigrants would have no difficulty in settling on the land or obtaining a lease and getting assistance from the owners of the land in order to get employment on the land.

I do not think it is too late to suggest to the miriister that he should withdraw this resolution, so that hon. members may study it and become more familiar with it. It is rather a radical move, a move that I would expect from my hon. friends from my left rather than from the Minister of the Interior. At least it is establishing something new that would have a bad effect on the public treasury. I am sure if the minister would withdraw the resolution beAvould be doing the country a kindness. It is all right to laugh, but at the same time you are loading up the industrial world and the country generally with something that it cannot. carry, as an hon. member stated a short time ago. The government is getting into difficulties all over, with rural credits, pensions and everything else that is being suggested. Who is going to carry the burden? I do not wish to talk about it. I think the minister should use his judgment and withdraw the resolution. It is a radical move, this suggestion to spoon-feed the people.
The Conservative government are doing it in England.
I do not care what they are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Ithinkthere is a great deal of misapprehension about the resolution. I do not see the danger suggested by my hon. friend who has just spoken. While the losses in connection with the activities of the Soldier Settlement Board have been large and will be larger, after all the board has served a very useful purpose
in Canada. No one will deny that. The difficulty to-day with the man going upon the land is that he has not got money. It is all right to talk about the ease with which a _ man can secure an improved farm. I know all about that. I have some farms I would not mind selling to someone on crop payments, without any payment down, but I could not afford to sell them for nothing,. Incidentally, while a man is working a farm on crop payments, he must have at least $2,000 with which to purchase stock and implements before he can farm the land. So that he is met at every corner with a handicap. There is inherent in the human mind, no matter where we go, a desire to own land, whether in the city or in the country. It is a laudable ambition, because the ownership of land ties a man to the land and to the country and makes him a much more valuable citizen than he would be if he had no ties or stake in the country. I want to encourage not only the young man in the country, but those who are in the cities and towns at the present time, to go out and procure land which they will have a reasonable chance of owning within a certain length of time.
I think I can safeguard this legislation so thoroughly that the loss will be reduced to the minimum. I do not mean to say that when the government directly advances say from two to four thousand dollars by way of farm loans upon an improved farm, it is not taking a considerable chance in regard to the repayment of the loan. The loan companies lose a great deal of money, and they exercise much care. When you go into it on such a scale you sometimes lose money. But when you have an encumbrance on the land and the land is the property of the crown; when all you are doing is trying to give the man a sufficient amount to carry him along as he improves that land, and when you provide a safeguard by ensuring that he does not get more than the value of the improvements he places upon the land, the chances of loss are reduced to a minimum.
How much does the minister think it would cost, roughly, on an average to clear this land per acre?? I know he cannot give exact figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If someone was hired to do the work it would probably cost $5 to $7.50 an acre. If the settler does it himself, the cost represents exactly the amount of energy he puts into the work, but we may say it would cost him on an average $5 an acre to clear that bush land. We have cleared whole townships of it in Al-
Advances to Settlers

berta by burning. There is a very prosperous settlement that I know well on the Edmonton-Dunvegan railway where three townships were burned over by officers of the Department of the Interior and were cleared very rapidly in that way. That is exceptionally easy' clearing, and probably it did not cost us more than twenty-five cents an acre to do it. Generally speaking there is sufficient timber on these lands to provide for the erection of log buildings. Many of these settlers would not under any circumstance get the maximum advance, but the advances would keep them at work improving their land whereas otherwise they would have to leave and finally abandon the land because they would have to go out in order to earn sufficient money to support their wives and families.
All a man would have after three years would be his wages, which would be paid by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not necessarily, because in my experience in western Canada, although this may not be true in the east, every homesteader has an opportunity during at least two months in the year of earning very high wages. During the last few years he has been earning, in harvesting operations and threshing, five to six dollars a day, with board; so that he earns a very respectable amount of money in that way in a very short time. This is merely supplemental in order to keep him on the land until the spring when he can best perform his duties, and to encourage him, if it is possible to do so, to own the land and to become a contented settler.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Clause 5 reads:
That no settlement loan shall be made upon the security of improvements upon any provincial crown land, unless tihe province by appropriate legislation, has provided that the improvements upon the security of which any such loan ds made shall be subject to a first charge for the amount of such loan with interest, and that no patent shall be issued for the said land until such loan with interest is repaid in full.
I do not see very much security that is going to be given in that way. In the first place the Minister of Justice may take care that his province will not permit the minister to put a federal mortgage on provincial crown land, and next if the province withholds the crown patent until the loan >is paid, supposing the loan is never paid how is the government going to get title? Suppose, for example, in the case of crown land in Ontario a loau is made and patent does not issue. AH the man mortgages is his right to a patent if ever he repays the loan. It is a sort of equity to title.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The arrangement will be between the provincial government and the federal government in that respect.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I know, but that is the basis of the arrangement as outlined in the resolution. All the province agrees to is that it will not issue patent until the loan is paid and that the loan will be a first charge. The province holds the patent; all the man mortgages is his right to patent once the loan is paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
But the
land would not be patented to anybody. The loan would be a prior claim on the land.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How is the government going to get title if the loan is not paid? There is no way in the world that it can get title. A man settles in northern Ontario, and the provincial government have passed legislation in Ontario that first of all if he borrows from the federal government the loan will be a first charge. They pass legislation also that they will not issue a patent until the loan to the federal government is paid. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The bulk of the land is in the prairie provinces and is vested in the federal government. As I pointed out this afternoon, the provincial governments of Ontario and Quebec have adopted a similar scheme for the settlement of their crown lands.

speechtext:
I did not

That is what I am particularly interested in. I have knowledge of some of the territory in the western provinces. I do not know whether the lands I have in mind are vested in the crown or not; that is why I put my question. Do any of the lands east of the city of Winnipeg along the Canadian National lines come into this scheme?

speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is some crown land there. Practically all lands in the northern portion of the three prairie provinces have been inspected by the inspectors of the Soldier Settlement Board. Those lands do not include any acreage such as I gave this afternoon. For example, out of a million acres in Saskatchewan, between 300,009 and 400,000 acres have been inspected by the Soldier Settlement Board inspectors, who have recommended the land, which is mostly brush and woodland, as suitable for settlement. In Manitoba I think land in five or six different localities has been inspected. In Alberta the Soldier Settlement Board inspectors have inspected five or six hundred thousand acres of land, mostly covered with timber and brush, that they recommend as being suitable for settlement. Those are the lands I have particularly in mind.

I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that the committee recognizes two things at least : that the problem with which we are faced to-day is the result, first, of the absolute lack of any proper system of colonization, of any proper principles. The orderly development of the city of Edmonton was tied up for years by the great block of land held by the Hudson's Bay Company and we were forced in consequence to extend our various utilities to reach the settled parts in the outskirts of the city. The committee recognizes also, I think, the sincerity and earnestness of the minister in charge of this proposal, and that he really conceives it to be a serious attempt to solve the problem. I do not like to criticize his proposal, although in point of fact criticism is the prerogative of the opposition and the price of office, but it seems to me that the government is indulging in an agricultural experiment which is going to mean nothing but a harvest of political disappointment and a financial loss to the country.
Before dealing with the elements of the proposal, may I mention one or two statements made by the minister which are misleading? In the first place, he spoke of the proposal as being a settlement, and the settlers as being settled under the act. I do not understand that there is any such thing as a settlement under the proposed act. The act, if it is passed, will possibly bring certain settlers within its purview and the range of its benefits, but I do not understand the phrase "settlement under the act." So far as I can see, there is no such thing.

Advances to Settlers
The minister mentioned a fifteen-mile limit. I cannot find any reference to a fifteen-mile limit in the proposal as we have it before the committee. Perhaps the minister can discover it himself, but it has eluded me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is not there.

The minister also said that
this proposal was for the purpose of helping to put settlers on the land. That of course, is not correct: the settler is on the land before he gets any assistance at all. He may be on the land for some years before he is in a position to make application for a loan, as I hope to prove in a few minutes.
Finally, the minister talks about a charge on the land. He gave the committee to understand that the federal government would have, as security for the loans, a charge on the land. In no sense is that true. If the land belongs to the federal government, the federal government can have no charge upon its own land, and if it is provincial government land the federal government certainly can have no charge on it unless the provincial government actually gives such charge. What the federal government will have by way of security for any loans it makes under the scheme will be a kind of equitable claim or charge against the interest of the particular settler, an interest which is very vague and indeterminate; and the moment it is abandoned, that very moment the security goes, and the money along with the security, because the only thing that will be left will be the personal covenant or promise of the settler. When the settler abandons his land, therefore, his personal covenant becomes absolutely worthless.
It is necessary for the committee to have these facts clearly in mind, and not to labour under the delusion that moneys that will be advanced under the scheme will have behind them anything which we can properly call a land security, or any tangible security, or any security which, in point of fact, can be realized at all. The fact is that it will be absolutely in the power of the settler at any moment to extinguish the security merely by his leaving the homestead and throwing the land back on the government.
The minister has said that the purpose of the proposal is to settle crown lands within fifteen miles of the railways. He has gone further and assured us that the reason there is any such land still available is that homesteaders have passed it up long since and gone out into the country forty and fifty miles further on, rather than take them up. Why? They have passed these lands up either be-
[Mr. Bury.J
cause they were poor or because, although being rich lands, they were so heavily timbered that it did not pay to clear the ground. I take it for granted that the land that would be brought within the purview of the proposed act would be not poor, but very heavily timbered, land. The question arises, then, as to what it would cost to clear such land. The Minister of the Interior tells us that it would cost $5 an acre to dear it. I do not think that is correct. Hon. gentlemen to my left understand something about clearing land, and I leave it to their judgment whether I am not nearer the mark when I say that the cost of clearing the land would be more like $15 or $20 per acre. Of course it entirely depends on the weight and thickness of the timber. If land could be cleared at $5 an acre it would not now be available for homesteading if it is within fifteen miles of a railway. I do not think anyone will dispute that statement. I happened to be in the northern part of the country two or three years ago in the neighbourhood of the Lesser Slave lake, and I saw some homesteads there with heavy timber on them. It was beautiful land. I asked some of the settlers what it would cost to clear such land, and they said $40 an acre. "In the name of fortune", I said, "how can it possibly pay a man to clear land at $40 an acre? Would it not be infinitely better to pay $10 an acre to begin with and get land already cleared?" That is a question which will be readily answered. However, if what the Minister of the Interior suggests is correct, and if this land can be cleared at a cost of $5 an acre, it means that before the unforutnate man can get a loan of $500 he must clear ICO acres of land. If he does not clear the whole 100 acres then he must put up a fence and build a house by way of improvement, which would mean that probably he would be on the farm about three years at the very least before he would have such improvements as would be worth $500. When he would have made improvements that would be worth $1,000 I leave it to the committee to imagine.
There is one other thing the committee must keep in mind. The minister has suggested that improved farms are so valuable in Alberta that a man has no difficulty in raising a loan of $600. I can only tell him that I lent a man personally $250 on an improved farm in Alberta near a railway station, and although that was ten years ago I am still whistling for the $250. In my office I am attending to two files representing mortgages, one of which started with a loan of $450 on a farm within a quarter of a mile of the rail-

Advan-ces to Settlers
way station. That was an improved farm and I cannot get any money out of it. I have another farm up in the Peace river district in which there is a loan of about $800 and it will keep me scratching to get my money out of that transaction. And these are all improved farms. The truth of the matter is that by reason of the fall in land values there are plenty of improved farms in Alberta that can be sold cheap, and I feel very much inclined to support the suggestion made by an hon. member to my left, whose constituency I cannot name, that it would be better for the government not to try to clear these heavily timbered lands but, if they are going to do anything in the direction now suggested, rather to assist in putting improved farms that are now derelict back into occupation and use. The settling of heavily timbered lands might come later, when through an increase in population in the immediate neighbourhood, the general price of land goes up and when there may be a greater market for the timber, so that those who might take them up could get something of appreciable worth from the clearing of the land itself. But to tackle the problem in the way the government now proposes, means, to my mind, that this country will be faced again with another fiasco and with a burden of debt. In Alberta we have seen the results of attempts to assist the agricultural industry. We had a famous cow bill once, the provisions of which all parties in Alberta united in passing.
Who was the author of it?

The Liberal government was
the author of that cow bill, but to be perfectly fair, I must say that the Conservative members of the House ardently supported it when it was brought forward. But nobody mentions the cow bill now except with bated breath or when no one is around.
It is all very well to talk of advancing money only to the extent of the actual improvements, and it is all very well to have your valuators go on the land to find out what the actual improvements are, but will the committee remember this: that the improvements on which they are proposing to advance this money are wasting improvements, that when a man steps out of his land, the breaking goes back into the old condition and becomes grass,	or worse still,	weeds. the roof goes, then the walls, and finally there is just about as much left to mark the place where those buildings and outbuildings were as there is over the site of Sodom and Gomorrah.
