What is the check on it?
They have to make certain improvements, and the most they can receive is $1,000.

Does the hon. member not
agree that the fewer the number that take advantage of this scheme, the less useful it is? His very argument that it is going to be taken advantage of by only a very few surely means that the scheme is going to be of very little use.

I think the hon. member
has not caught the point. I say this scheme will be taken advantage of by a certain class of people who have not sufficient capital to go on what I would call a really good cleared farm. It will appeal to men who are working out by the day during the summer and going back to the farm in the winter and making their improvements. My hon. friend from East Edmonton said that when one of these farms is vacated the fence posts and even the doors and windows of the houses are stolen by the neighbours. If there was anything else left, Mr. Chairman, I think the lawyers would get it.
That is why I am so poor.

I was rather surprised, I
will not say at the indignation shown by the hon member for St. 'Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) this 'afternoon, because I believe he was quite in earnest when he spoke of the terrible burdens the east was carrying for the west. This was only another scheme, in his view, whereby millions would be loaded on to the shoulders of the eastern people. Mr. Chairman, I do not know when this sort of talk, this everlasting story of the east carrying the west upon its shoulders, is going to end. I have borrowed money sometimes, I suppose from eastern capitalists, and I never got it for less than 8 per cent. I never supposed there was any favour in the thing; it was simply a business transaction, and if hon. members in the east have made bad investments in western Canada it must have been through their want of sound business judgment. I cannot understand this constant talk of the east bearing the burdens of the west, of every move made in western Canada as being something that is going to be a further burden on the

shoulders of the east. I deplore that sort of talk, and I think we ought to stop it. The people of the three western prairie provinces do not want any charity; all they want is fair play and a square deal.

They take all that
is coming to them.

You do not hear us talking that way of eastern Canada. You do not hear any western man finding fault with the east or with the Maritime provinces. We are 'perfectly ready to help the east and the Maritime provinces in every way we can. Furthermore, I say this talk does not make for a united Canada, and I want to see a united Canada. I want this talk of east and west, of one carrying the burdens of the other, to stop, because I do not believe there is anything in it.
May I ask the hon. member how he expects to have a united Canada in the face of the Speech from the Throne that this government brought down this year?

How often hon. members
are pointing across the floor and saying, "this" government. This government is here, and apparently it is going to stay here for some time.

Does the hon. member think
that he should have been pointed to instead?

I am not going to take up
very much time, and I hope hon. members will allow' me to finish. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is now in his seat, and I wish to relieve his mind a little. I want to tell him there is no danger that the east is going to be swamped by "this little insignificant attempt that is being made at the present time to help some of the workingmen to get homesteads out in western Canada or in any of the other provinces. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-iSt. George-1 an repeating this just for his benefit-seemed to get very much worked up this afternoon about the tremendous burden that was being heaped on the shoulders of the eastern people through some of the commitments that are being made in western Canada. Mr. Chairman, I repeat that I repudiate any such statement. I know something about the history of railroad building and of the opening up of western Canada. I have seen that part of the west in which I live develop from the prairie to the point that we have there now a civilized community; we have roads and bridges, rural mail deliv-

Advances to Settlers
ery, and all the conveniences of modern civilization. I know something about western Canada, and I think we ought to stop this talk about the east carrying all the burdens for the west.
What remedy do these critics propose in place of the scheme that we are now considering? Hon. members continually repeat the assertion that what we want to-day in this Dominion is a larger population. We want more people, they say. What are we going to do with them? I wish the hon. members who make this statement so frequently would tell us what we can do with them.

I will tell my hon. friend,
if he will permit me. We are bringing into this country $600,000,000 of foreign products that can be manufactured in the Dominion.
I had an idea what my hon. friend would suggest before he made his statement.
Quite so.

A great many arguments have been advanced during the last four years in an effort to prove the truth of that assertion. I have as yet failed to see that it will remedy the problems we have to meet. We are producing more goods than we can sell now, and they are being produced at a cost which renders it impossible to compete with other countries. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George would restrict the buying power of the people of Canada by forcing them to buy the goods that are produced here, notwithstanding the price at which they are produced.
Be patriotic.

I am just as patriotic as
hon. gentlemen who adopt that line of argument. But I am convinced that even if those hon. gentlemen had their way and obtained increased protection, that would not solve the problems with which we are now confronted. If any hon. member who favours that argument will give it serious thought he will soon come to the conclusion that his theory will not solve our problems. We have heard it stated, and it has been repeated time and time again, that we have all the facilities necessary to carry on business for twice our population, and that we need population to help to bear the capital expenditure that has been made in procuring those facilities. Now I come back to the question as to what we are going to do with the population we now have. You do not want them in the towns;
you say you have not markets enough now for the goods you are producing in the industrial centres, and that you want to create a greater market in this Dominion. How are you going to create that market? By an increased population engaged in creating natural wealth. Now, I want to draw a distinction, Mr. Chairman, between what I call creating natural wealth and creating industrial wealth, because there is quite a difference between the two. I want hon. members to understand that I do not belittle in any way the production of wealth by industrial methods. Industry adds to the value of an article by shaping it so that it will be available for the actual use of humanity. Wealth derived directly from the soil is actually created wealth. Not only that, but the soil produces wealth that pays for the employment necessary to its production. These are the A B C's of economics, and no one who has studied the subject for a moment can fail to understand them.
The great problem before us to-day then, is to increase our population, and the only way in which that can be successfully done is by increasing our agricultural population. How are you going to do that? By making those who are already living on the soil industrious and contented. Now we get back to the basis of the whole theory that has brought this section of the House into parliament. I want to make the statement here that this is no sectional or narrow view: I honestly believe that the whole economic structure of our country is built upon an agricultural basis. I am not for a moment arguing that agriculture is everything in Canada. But let me say this: make agriculture prosperous and you will solve the problem we have before us.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George told us that the per capita wealth of western Canada was much greater than the per capita wealth of eastern Canada. Well, I am sorry the hon. gentleman was not in the House when the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) was speaking, because he told us about some farms of a few hundred acres on which there were mortgages, that the mortagees had never been able to pay off. There is something wrong in that line of reasoning. On the one hand they are unable to pay off the mortgages on those farms in the west, and on the other hand the west has a larger per capita wealth than the east.

We have some in the east as well.

An. hon. member asks me
what about the people in the towns. I claim that if things are carried on as they ought to be in the west the people in the towns will be exactly in the same position. If there is more wealth in the cities than there is in the rural districts in western Canada it is because there is something economically wrong. That should not be the case.
I did not intend to make a speech when , I rose, but I want to repeat that there is nothing in this scheme that is alarming, nothing that is going to saddle the country with very much additional debt. I do think, however, it will afford an opportunity for a class of people we have in western Canada, men who work by the day and gather up perhaps four or five hundred dollars in the harvest and threshing time, to get back to their quarter section, if they have one, and spend the winter months in improving and clearing that scrub land. Not only that, but such a man will be able to provide a home for his wife and his children. He may be able even to keep a certain number of chickens and a cow or two. I say there is nothing very alarming about the proposal. It will open up certain districts for settlement for a class of men who will not be able to undertake farming on a more ambitious scale.

I understand the hon. member was president of the Union of Municipalities in Manitoba for some years, and has had experience in connection with the tying up of unpatented lands from a municipal point of view. How does he suggest that this scheme is going to help development in the western country?
The situation cannot be any worse than it is, because these lands are not paying taxes now.
Until the settlers get on them they do not, but the moment they do you increase the municipal expense without providing the municipality with any source of revenue.

I do not see that there is
any difficulty there, because if a man is settled on a quarter section of land and earning money at all the taxes on that character of land ought to be very low. The municipality would thus be in a safer position than if the land were lying idle and unoccupied.

I do not rise for
the purpose of opposing the resolution, but I think the government should proceed very

cautiously in this direction. The venture of lending money to settlers is not new in this country. A few years ago an act was passed under which moneys were loaned to returned soldiers. If I remember rightly that was done under the Soldier Settlement Act. I am speaking from memory now, but I think that under that act something like SI00,000,000- the minister tells me 8102,000,000-were loaned to returned soldiers. The wisdom of lending money to settlers was the same then as it is now, but at the time that act was passed the paramount argument was that returned soldiers had to be helped and that the country should be in a position to assume whatever risks such loans would entail. In my opinion that was the chief argument; that was the main reason. The government that promoted the legislation at that time should have been blamed very severely, because experience has proven that through this scheme of lending money to the settlers the country is losing each year enormous amounts of money. There is no question that out of the 8100,000,000 that was loaned to soldiers a very large amount will never be collected and will be lost. I am not saying this by way of criticism, but I wish to point out that the venture of lending money to settlers is not new, and now that we have had the experience of one venture of the kind; now that we know the result which can be achieved by our lending money to settlers, I can hardly understand the wisdom of going into a new venture of making advances, not to soldiers, but to settlers generally-civilians. If one will make a study of these loans to returned soldiers, one may very well imagine that similar conditions will obtain under this loan. Soldiers have borrowed money, but after one, two or three years they found they could not continue on the land; they had to abandon their farms and go away, and some of the farms became practically worthless. Soldiers have borrowed money in some cases in excess of the value of the farm; of course that was the fault of the officials who recommended the loan. In many cases they have been unable to repay, and what are you going to do with them? Are you going to take their farms away from them? Are you going to bring actions in law against them? You can hardly do that. What I am saying with regard to the soldiers applies with greater force to the civilians. The same difficulties which have been encountered with soldiers will be encountered with civilians, and that is why I state that the wisdom of this legislation is faulty.

He may do what ninety-five per cent of the homesteaders in western Canada have done already. They had some indebtedness; they paid it off and obtained a loan, generally about $800, sometimes paying eight per cent and sometimes nine. This scheme is for a different purpose; it is to lend them money on the progress they make in clearing up their land and making it of some value, to bring their homestead to a stage where perhaps they can get through with a very much smaller loan than they have had to negotiate in the past. That is the only difference between this scheme and rural credits.
In reply to the hon. member for East Edmonton, I have seen a great deal of what he has stated as having happened in the case of the homesteaders-not altogether in the case of the homesteaders, because he has reference to the secondary stage, in which there was a mortgage on the land, and of course the mortgage was a detriment to the new settler taking advantage of the scheme of purchase. It has* always been so; it is true every day. These lands will remain in the crown, with a mortgage against them; why? Because it is better business to go back thirty
miles from a railway and take up land, than to buy lands lying close to railway facilities or close to towns, and pay the claims that may be against them. Where the land remains in the crown, where it is subject to re-entry, if it is worth anything at all it does not remain very long in that position. I am not going to argue that in the ease of the man who abandons his land, say having earned $500, the same condition will not apply. The new homesteader might rather take his chance on a homestead entirely free from encumbrance than one carrying a small mortgage with nine per cent interest attached.
I am not claiming that I have discovered anything new or striking about this matter, but I do claim that if judiciously applied, on reasonably good land, it will assist materially in the settlement of that land. Even in our province, in the newer territory back of Peace river, where you have a good climate and good open land, you can obtain all kinds of homesteads, but that entails expenditure of money for the construction of new railways. I have always been opposed to that; when in the provincial government of Alberta I did my best to discourage the spreading of settlement, because it entailed the building of roads and schools to serve sparse settlements over large areas of land. That has been our practical difficulty in western Canada ever since I knew it. I do hope the rural credit scheme will consolidate settlement where we have land privately owned in the hands of the people, or even in the hands of prospective purchasers, because we hope to settle 1,200 families from the Old Country on improved lands under the arrangement we have with the British government. These lands are all in the hands of the Soldier Settlement Board at the present time, and that may relieve the somewhat difficult situation there. The rural credit scheme will help the farmer who finds it difficult, at the present high rates of interest, to remain on his land. I am going to ask hon. members, in the next bill that comes up, to consider some provision for assistance to sbldier settlers, many of whom at present find themselves in a very serious position, which will enable them to remain on their land. All these things are designed with a view to thickening up settlement, to using the railways for which we have already paid, and to assisting materially in building up the country itself. If the committee will allow this resolution to pass I will, having in mind some of the suggestions made by hon. gentlemen, have the bill amended in that respect before it is given its second reading.

I asked the hon. member for Brandon a few moments ago to answer what seemed to be a very pertinent question in view of the remarks which he had just been extending towards members of parliament from eastern Canada. I invite his serious consideration of that question which I asked of him, and I invite him to reply to it on the floor of this House. But it is not for that purpose that I rise now. Dealing directly with the resolution which is now before the chair, and having regard to the remarks made by the hon. member for East Edmonton a few minutes ago, I should like to know the real purpose of this legislation.
I may be obtuse; I may not know conditions in the west, but the real necessity for this legislation is not apparent to me and to a large number of other hon. members. Is it to take care of a situation which has arisen as a result of the soldier settlement scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Then what is it? In other words, to use the language of the hon. member for East Edmonton, what is the oblique influence behind this legislation causing this government to embark on a money-lending scheme? I take it that it is sound governmental practice for a government to keep out of the money-lending business. We have done altogether too much of it in Canada; we are paying the piper to-day and posterity will pay the piper to-morrow.
There is another feature in connection with this contemplated settlement of crown lands in the provinces. I do not know what the practice is in the older provinces of Ontario and Quebec, but I do know something about the practice in New Brunswick. They have a system of settlement of crown lands in that province under what is known as the Labour Act. A would-be settler on crown lands goes in and makes his clearance. He is given practically as many years as he likes, but he must clear and cultivate ten acres and erect a building on it. When he does that he is entitled to a free grant of 160 acres of land, but until he does that he gets no patent. The process is a long, slow one, because most of that land is heavily timbered and it costs not $20 but $50 or $100 an acre to clear it. The would-be settler does this work at odd times, for instance in the spring of the year. He bums what he calls his fallow and he clears it up gradually while he is doing other work.
Has the minister consulted members of the provincial governments in regard to this

scheme? Does he think it will be taken advantage of by any of the older provinces?
I do not think for a minute it will be of the slightest advantage to any single province in eastern Canada, but with all due respect to the opinion of the hon. member for Brandon I think we shall pay the major part of the bill. I would not object to that so much if there was any real foundation for the belief that it would be a success, because I realize, as most men do who have been in this House for any number of years, that we must get more people on the land in Canada and make it profitable for them to stay there.
I know that in the older parts of Canada there are many fertile farms which might be peopled with good settlers if they had some form of proper assistance. This is not the class of scheme that will bring about that result.	.
What is the expert opinion of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell)? He is never very slow to give us the benefit of his advice. Has he examined into this scheme? What has he to say about it? I cannot conscientiously vote for this scheme unless I find that it has his imprimatur, and I invite him now to get up and give us the benefit of his views, having regard not only to the three prairie provinces, including the one which he represents, but to the other great provinces of this Dominion, the new provinces as well as the old ones. Let us hear from the Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I could not resist such a pressing invitation to say something on this subject although I thought it was receiving ample attention from the various members of the House. The committee will recall that during the last four years this government has been subject to a great deal of adverse criticism by my hon. friends opposite and their press because we were not doing some-9 p.m. thing to promote immigration to Canada. As a matter of fact it was said that the number of immigrants was getting less and that apparently not very much was being done. In 1920, immediately after the close of the war, there was a tremendous deflation in agricultural prices and this rendered agriculture for a number of years quite unprofitable to those who were here and well established. The years 1921, 1922 and 1923 particularly were years of loss and in some cases of disaster to many farmers in Canada, .although perhaps they were no worse off, if not better off, than farmers in other countries. But it was not a good time to take a forward step in promoting immigration to this country, for the simple reason that immigrants would experience tremendous dif-

Advances to Settlers
ficuilty in getting established under the conditions that prevailed during those three years. Since then conditions have changed; prices have got better, and we have experienced . two or three good crops. That, accompanied by good management and thrift on the part of the farmers themselves, has brought about better financial conditions amongst the farmers generally. That, in turn, has had its effect on immigration; prospective immigrants in larger numbers are desirous of coming to our shores, and the government feels justified at this time in encouraging them to come because conditions are such that they should be able to make a success. That is briefly why we are taking an advanced step at this time as against not taking it in 1921. At that time it would have been unfortunate to place on the land people with practically no money and, expect them to make good under conditions under which old settlers, well established, found it difficult to succeed. Judging from the criticism of some hon. members one would think that this is a radical departure. It is not. For the last forty years we have given some form of assistance to homesteaders, especially in the west; not of this nature, it is true, but after they got on their homesteads how many times has seed grain been given to them, as well as fodder for their animals and food for themselves, in addition to loans of one description and another? That is no new thing.

That assistance was not
part of a settlement scheme; it was given to meet abnormal conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Let me go back
further than that. A hundred years ago the government assisted settlers to establish themselves in the woods of Ontario and other parts o:f Canada, the assistance taking the form of loans, equipment and tools. Quite frequently those loans were wiped off to still further encourage the settlers. In a word,, it was found necessary in order to encourage settle-, ment to give some form of assistance that settlers might establish themselves in this new land. Surely that was good work, Mr. Chairman. From that day down to this some form of assistance has been held out to settlers to establish themselves on the land1. To-day, even if you igive the maximum loan under this resolution, it is not as much of an attraction as the governments of Canada have been holding out for the last thirty or forty years in the form of free homesteads on the open plain. Such a homestead as used to be available fifteen or twenty years ago was
worth more as a drawing card for settlers than the average homestead of to-day plus the maximum loan under this bill.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, no scheme can be evolved that is not subject to some form of criticism. The right hon. leader of the opposition was true to himseltf to-day as he pictured the gall and wormwood of disappointment that would follow when we tried to collect the loans to be granted under this scheme. No lending scheme either by a private individual or by a government has been carried out without some loss; that is inevitable. Now, are we to refrain from encouraging settlement on our vacant lands because there is a possibility of some of the loans not being .repaid? No. I think the time is ripe when we should go forward and endeavour to people the great waste spaces in western Canada and other parts of the Dominion. Those who are likely to come to Canada at this time are not men of extensive means. If they have substantial means I fancy they are not going to embark on farming just yet; there are other attractions. Consequently our settlers will be men of limited means. The first step the government took under the Minister of the Interior to promote this forward movement was in the reduction of the ocean and railway transportation rates for settlers. It now costs three pounds sterling to land them at Halifax as against at least twice that much in former years. The next step is to hold out a drawing card that will attract them just as a good plains homestead did twenty or twenty-five years ago. Naturally risks will have to be taken in connection with this work. Such security as is available will be taken, but with this difference from an ordinary loan, that the money will not be paid out to the settler until it is warranted by his having established himself on the land, that is by building a home, digging a well, and so on, in order to enable him to go on his farm with his family. It is well known that few men went out to the west with anything but the clothes on their back and a keen desire to work. Ordinarily those men were not able to bring out their families for two or three years. Under this scheme a settler will be able to put up his shack and stable and bring out his family without delay,-and farming is a pretty slavish uphill business to a man struggling along alone.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
How will he bring his
family out when he gets his loan only on the security of the improvements he has made?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There is one thing sure, 'he will be able to bring them out sooner as a result of the loan. And what is more, the very fact that he is able to stay on his * homestead and put up his house without having to go out to work and earn the money is surely in his favour.

How can he use the money
to put up his house and make his improvements if he does not get his loan until those improvements are all made?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Now, Mr. Chairman, the lawyers can quibble and squirm about this all they like but I have gone through it all.
Will the hon. minister tell me just exactly how it can be done because it will be worth money.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I know it can be done, it has been done and it will be done better with a little aid than without any.
Will the hon. minister tell me 'how to do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Well, as I listened
to my hon. friend describe the emaciated condition of his own clients, I was thinking that his speech would not help to bring any immigrants to Canada. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, if our friends opposite would just realize that their gloomy forebodings will counteract the effects of all our aid,-
Some hon. M(EMBERS: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That is the fact. Certainly any prospective immigrant will be discouraged who may have the bad fortune to read the dispiriting speeches by my hon. friends opposite that the loans under this proposal will be squandered by the settlers and only a few ruins be left on the prairie to mark where once houses and stables stood. If my hon. friends think that their gloomy talk will promote land settlement, I do not agree with them. I think the time has come when we should discuss this question from the standpoint of actually promoting the settlement of our vacant lands.
I notice there is a tendency to take the ground that what our people want is work. Will any homesteader in this chamber tell me any better way of giving a man work than by putting him on a homestead? Did you ever see a farmer or a homesteader out of a job? I never did. My hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) and another hon. member, I think my friend from St.

Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), put it very nicely when they suggested that what we wanted was industry. Well, that gets us back to the old question of protection. Now, I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if the early British settlers who were brought out here shortly after the Napoleonic wars found industries established here? Did the British government first attempt to establish industries in this part of the world, or was not their primary anxiety to get settlers on the land, which would eventually necessitate the establishing of industries to supply their various requirements?	*
Mr. BENNETT; The minister knows they had protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It is simply putting the cart before- the horse. Industries came later. And so to-day we must first get men on the land, and then the supplying of their needs will necessitate the establishment of more industries or the speeding up of those we already have. Consequently work must come at the beginning, because the man on a homestead is never known to be out of a job; industries will come later.
I think the Minister of the Interior is working along right lines. This is a modest beginning. I can understand my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition being somewhat wary of even these small loans, because he has gone through the somewhat excruciating experience associated with the soldier settlement scheme which I think he was partly responsible for. I do not want to criticize that scheme severely, because it was undertaken with the best intention to be kind to the soldiers; but it loaded them up with debts running from $5,000 to $7,000. Those of us on the prairies had misgivings, and I stated mine to the gentleman who had charge of the board and who seemed to agree with me. I said I thought it was better to go slow rather than to go head over heels into debt; I did not think that more than one out of three or four of the soldiers who got these large loans would ever be able to extricate themselves from their indebtedness. Unfortunately that has come true, and we must be wary about any proposal of the kind. But under the present scheme the largest loan will be $1,000, and under proper administration, as I am sure this will be, very few will take advantage of the maximum loan. The British settlers under this arrangement will dovetail into the empire settlement scheme. Settlers from Great Britain eligible for the $500 loan will come under the provisions of that scheme, and that is one great advantage of this pro-

Advances to Settlers
posal. The others will be immigrants of various extraction, many of whom will not require any loans at all. Probably a good many of them will never make any application, for they will homestead very economically. If there is no timber they will put up a sod shack, as I have seen done. I live in a neighbourhood adjoining a town called Lemberg, and from the name one can form an idea of the origin and character of the settlers. I saw them go in there thirty years ago, and all the shelter they had was a teepee of willows tied at the top with a withe, Indian-fashion. That was the only house they had, and a little later they put up a sod shack. They progressed as time went on, and to-day the settlement is one of the most prosperous in Saskatchewan. They have fine houses with all modern conveniences, such as the telephone, and many of them have radios. They are largely out of debt into the bargain.
One of the greatest, I was almost going to say curses, to agriculture, in the prairies at any rate, has been too indiscriminate a tendency on the part of the people to go into debt. Formerly they would quarrel with the mortgage companies if they could not get another thousand added to the burden they already carried. That day has passed. We are getting away from that condition, and I hope there will not be a repetition of that orgy of reckless borrowing. Moderate borrowing is a blessing, for it can be controlled. But excessive borrowing has ruined agriculture in many instances, and to-day we are suffering from that curse.
Now, the moderate loans suggested in this proposal will have this effect, at least, of bringing people to a realization of what it means to pay back even a small amount. They will have to pay back the first loan before they can put on a second mortgage. This will be the means of steadying the borrower, so that he will not be overburdened with a debt which he will find it impossible to discharge. That is one incidental advantage in the scheme. I see the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George smiling. Let me assure him that I am not advancing any arguments; I am simply stating what I know to be a fact. I know quite well that fifteen years or so ago, men unwittingly drifted into debt to such an enormous extent that they found themselves unable afterwards to meet their obligations, and they did this under the delusion that by some turn of fortune they would be enabled to wipe out their indebtedness. They find today, however, that only by the sweat of their brow in a fearfully arduous task will they
ever be able to pay their debts. The beginning under this system will be modest, and, as I have said, there wrill be many who will probably require no assistance at all.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

I see my hon
friend (Mr. Hanson) laughing; I can understand his doing so. This is Greek to him.
I want to assure the minister that I was not laughing at him.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not want to be uncomplimentary, but I do not expect my hon. friend to understand a word of what I am saying.
I protest I was not laughing at the minister at all. I was laughing at something that was said over here.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I could not understand anything about an involved technical constitutional question; I should be just as ignorant of such a subject as the hon. member is of the matter I am now discussing. Now, Mr. Chairman, I think I have covered the field pretty well.
Go on.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Oh, no. I have got through and I think it is time to quit.

I do not
want to take up much time, but I am in doubt as to where the government stands on this matter. I believe there is an understanding between the main wing of the Liberal party and the minor wing to my left in regard to all legislation brought into the House, and I presume that under that arrangement this subject has been duly submitted at least to the member for Brandon, the leader of the Progressive party in this House. But my understanding of what has been said by the Minister of the Interior, so beautifully amplified and clarified by the Minister of Agriculture, is entirely different from my understanding of the remarks of the hon. member for Brandon. If I have followed the Minister of the Interior correctly, the idea of the scheme is to put men on the land to work it and became farmers on their own account. No, says the member for Brandon, that is not the idea at all. He does not expect that this splendid scheme, which he endorses thoroughly, will result in many people going on the land. The hon. member for Brandon tells us that if they do go on the land they will spend their time working for other farmers. In other words, the building which they will put up on th'"
Advances to Settlers

land they acquire will' be merely the place they will live in. They are not going to work their own land themselves. These people, according to the hon. member, will keep two or three cows and a few chickens, and while they work out for other farmers the family at home, the good wife and the children, will look after these cows and chickens. That is the way they are going to make their money.
Well, that brings us to the point of the special appeal that will be made in propaganda, disseminated throughout the world, to induce settlers to come in and take up fend under this proposal. The government, backed up by the member for Brandon, will send out literature, calling attention to the splendid opportunity offering for men to come to this country to settle upon the land. And the hon. member for Brandon will add to that advertisement a little explanation as to the splendid wealth immigrants will amass from raising chickens and keeping two or three cows. He will point out that under this government's policy intending immigrants will be able to produce eggs and sell them in competition with eggs coming from Australia and New Zealand free of duty, or with eggs imported from China, or from the United States under a duty of three cents a dozen. He will make that perfectly clear to them, and it will be a strong inducement to them to come in and take up land. I suppose he will go on to point out the opportunities for acquiring ready cash and becoming rich which will be afforded1 by the production of butter in competition with butter coming in from Australia and New Zealand at a cent a pound. . All this will ibe quite attractive, and it will undoubtedly draw thousands of people to this country. My hon. friend from Brandon will be there waiting with a smile to convince the immigrants when they come that the way to get rich in this country in farming is that provided by the policy which he has followed, the policy of buying everything which the farmers require at protected prices and selling in competition with the whole world without any protection whatever. That is his idea of the way to make them prosper in this country. The minister informs us that he expects to get people to settle on the land under this plan. The hon. member for Brandon says:	I am
heart and soul behind this proposition; it is a good thing, but I do not expect very many people will take advantage of it. His position, it seems to me, is absolutely illogical and absolutely unreasonable. I think that a good deal can be said in favour of trying
(Mr. J. W. Edwards.]
to fill up the places which have been vacated in the older settled parts of the country; that is something we might very well attend to. But if you are going to encourage people to stay on the land you must giv3 those who do stay a square deal in regard to the selling of their products. That this government is not disposed to do, and I do not suppose ever will do, so long as it submits to the advice, not to say dictation, of the hon. member for Brandon.
Mr. MoLEAN (Melfort): Before the House rose for dinner, I was very much interested in listening to the very fair and reasonable criticisms particularly of the hon. member for West Calgary and the right hon. leader of the opposition. The hon. member for West Calgary saw certain dangers in this proposition as it is now drafted, and suggested that care would have to be taken, that possibly it would be well to cut down the amount of money that would be available at least for the first year, and that other safeguards of that kind should be provided. The minister immediately agreed to that, and I think it was well that he did so. I think the debate before six o'clock was eminently reasonable, but listening to the skilled agriculturists who have been speaking recently, and lecturing the farmers of (Manitoba on how and how not to do things on their land, it seems to me the tone of the debate has changed since dinner.
A good many criticisms have been offered during the course of the debate, some of them reasonable and some otherwise. Much has been made of the extensive losses incurred under the Soldier Settlement Board, and it has been suggested that if such losses were incurred under the direction of that Board, equally great losses in proportion would be incurred under this scheme. I do not agree. The Soldier Settlement Board started to function at a time when prices were at the peak of inflation, and they had to function at first with men who had not been trained to their jobs. I am not blaming them for |that, because no doubt they got the best men available, but, of course, they made mistakes, and largely through the mistakes they made were they able to learn. The soldier settlers who went on the land in the first flush of their return home, after having been overseas for so many years, were naturally anxious to get out of uniform and to go on the land, and perhaps they took land that did not appeal to them, and at prices and on terms that were not altogether satisfactory to them, but they were so anxious to get away from military life and regulations, so glad to.be their own masters once again, that many took chances

Advances to Settlers
that a few years later they would not have taken. Under those circumstances, with so many of these men heavily handicapped in taking up land at the time they did, the wonder to me, Mr. Chairman, is not that some of the soldier settlers did not make good, not that so much money has been lost, but that so many of them have made good in spite of the handicaps they were under. They were placed on land which was sold at high prices, and they stayed on the land during those years when times were not good even for the best of farmers, for men who had been on the land right along and had their equipment pretty well paid for and were off to a good start, but who have found it difficult financing in the past few years, commencing with the break in the price of wheat in 1920, and continuing for a few years thereafter. Yet the soldiers who bought their land at high, prices have in large numbers and in many districts stayed on the land, battled with their problems, and are to-day coming out on the right side. Many men were placed on crown lands at a distance from the railway, in settlements where there were no roads, no schools, no facilities, and no medical care for long distances, and yet a great percentage of these men have stayed with the game and are winning out. If they were able to do that without the aid of the very skilful organization which has been built up since, and which has got more careful and more skilful as time went on, it stands to reason that a settler going on crown lands to-day, with whatever help from this organization is necessary in the way of advice and inspection of his land before and after he makes his improvements, has a much better chance of success than those who bought land at the peak prices a few years ago. In view of the very different conditions, I do not think it is fair to compare the failures under the soldier settlement scheme with what some hon. gentlemen think might happen under this scheme.
I have been struck with this thought, that the hon. gentlemen who criticized this scheme before dinner, very reasonably and fairly, were men who know the Dominion of Canada as a whole. The eminent fanners opposite who have criticized the scheme since dinner do not, I think, know the Dominion as well as their leaders who spoke before them. There is much good land running right across northern Canada, from Quebec west. I am not speaking of the Maritime provinces because I do not claim to know so much about them. I have running through my
mind the words of an old Gaelic song written by a pioneer in the Maritime provinces, near Barney's river, in Nova Scotia. I do not know where Barney's river is; all I know about the place is what the song told me. This settler was afraid that before the trees were uprooted the strength would be gone out of his arm, that his back would be bowed before he could bring his land under cultivation and his children were able to make a living. I think that was a reasonable fear. The hon. member for York-Sunbury admitted a little while ago that in New Brunswick it is a slow process getting these lands cleared.
As I said a moment ago, there is much good land across northern Canada, in Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan, but it is a slow and a hard jub clearing these lands. But the land is good. Some hon. members seem to be under the misapprehension that this is second-class land. In many cases it is the very best of land, and it is because of the climatic conditions and the very fact that these lands were good for raising a crop that they have been left vacant so long. The crops having grown so strongly and vigorously, the land was not as easily put into another crop as would be the case in the drier districts in the prairie provinces, and so we find that much of the best land has been left to the last because of the crop of timber that has grown upon it. That good land stretches across five provinces, and it is to speed up the work of clearing this land, which the hon. member for York-Sunbury admitted was a slow job, that these proposed loans are being made.
How are these loans going to speed up the clearing of land?

'Suppose I go
on to a vacant piece of land in northern Ontario to-day, having in my possession fifty or a hundred dollars. I could not go very far in clearing land with that amount of money. Under this scheme I know that by the time I spend $50 or $100 in clearing land, erecting buildings, ditching, or doing whatever that particular piece of land happens to need, the services of the homestead inspector, or such officer of the department as is detailed for the duty, will be available. Now, these officers of the department are passing through the new districts in the course of their usual occupation; special trips would not be necessary all the time and therefore no great additional expense would be entailed on this account. Well, we will say that I have gone on the land and exhausted my $100. Then I apply for an inspection of the

Advances to Settlers
improvements. The officer comes there and sees that I have given value for the $100 or $150 as the case may be. In the course of a little time I get a warrant as a result of which that money is refunded to me. I then go ahead and use that money over again; it is a sort of perambulating fund. I take it that is the principle of the bill.
An hon. M;EMBER: That is not in the bill.

That may be,
but I think there is nothing in the bill to justify the conclusion that it is not the main principle involved.
We have not got the bill. We only have the resolution on which the bill will be drafted.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am trying to get the bill before the House.

We are considering a resolution, and after it has been adopted the bill will be placed before the House. The situation, as I see it, is this: that a man coming along with a little money would be allowed to spend that money on improvements, but it would be refunded to him as he spent it from time to time. \\ e pay him for what he does until he comes to the limit of his loan, either $1,000 or $500. That was the system employed in connection with the settlement of the land by soldier settlers. Under the Soldier Settlement Act the settler would go to the supervisor and say he wanted to sink a well, or put up a bam or a house, or carry out some other improvements. The supervisor, from his knowledge of local conditions and of the settler himself, could say, "All right, we will give you authority to do that . Then the settler would go ahead, breaking the land and carrying out other improvements, and so was able to make progress even under the handicaps from which he suffered.
One criticism was made, I think by the hon. member for East Edmonton. He said there was much land that could be bought cheaper than other lands could be homesteaded and cultivated. That is partly true, but if a man does not have money to buy a piece of land even if the land is cheap, he is subjected to a load of debt, and the accumulated charges are going to handicap him a great deal. Many a man would prefer to take a piece of land that would be hard to clear as long as that land was all right otherwise. He would prefer to wait a little while longer so as to keep out of debt as much as possible and finally get a clear title to it much sooner. In the 
case of a piece of land out in the open prairie the value might be $25 an acre. Well, that would be $4,000 for a quarter section, and the interest on it at nine per cent would be $360 a year, or a dollar for every day he was on it. Many men would prefer to go on a piece of raw land if it can be got from the Dominion for an entry fee of $10, and spend their time breaking and preparing it. In that case they would be able to establish a home at much less cost in cash than in the case of the land indicated by the hon. member for East Edmonton.
The criticism has been made that a settler would only have a home on such a piece of land. That is the greatest thing any citizen could have. There is no person coming from another countiy who would not be glad to have a home, accompanied by security of tenure in that home. In my opinion, and it is also the opinion of very many men more experienced than I am, if the people of Canada would do more to make real permanent homes for themselves and not be quite so anxious in the early years to make money they would get along in the world faster and go farther. That is the consensus of opinion among farmers to-day in the west, and I believe it is the reason why there is so much less credit being used; many people are satisfied to proceed a little more slowly and pav their way as they go.
The criticism has also been made that if this form of aid to settlement goes through assistance ought to be granted to men wishing to go into industry or business. Well, there is this difference between the two sets of cases in my opinion-that wherever there is a business opening, whether it is a retail store, a factory, a brokerage business, or anything else of that kind-plenty of applicants will be found ready to take advantage of the opportunity. Government assistance is not necessary m order to get a new business of that kind established on a small scale. But when it -comes to clearing these rougher lands of good quality, it cannot be reiterated too often that the state should do any little thing it can to make the process of settlement and home establishment speedier. Any steps of that character are proper steps, provided that due precautions are adopted in taking them.
The principle embodied in this resolution is not a new one. Scores of years ago the early settlers who came into Ontario were given assistance in the way of grubstakes, tools and other aids of that kind. The same thing was probably done in the Maritime provinces; certainly it was done in Ontario and, I think, in Quebec. Very little assistance

Advances to Settlers
of this character has been given in western Canada. Much criticism has been heard in past years in Canada in regard to the government doing such and so for men who came from other lands, whereas nothing was done for our own people, and the argument was advanced, "You have us here, but you will not do anything for us. You offer inducements to outsiders to come here." I think we are justified in giving perhaps a little bit more of assistance to our own citizens when they wish to go on the land. We have seen that when lands in the open prairie ceased to be free, men who wanted lands went into the more northerly districts where the land was harder to clear and kept plugging away, with the result that in a few years they had brought more land under cultivation than some of the older provinces have altogether. There will always be a market for foodstuffs. No nation ever had to go to war to sell its foodstuffs. Nations have to do many things to sell their manufactured goods; and much trouble has been wrought in the world by nations hunting for new markets. I do not think you will ever find an instance recorded where nations had to go to war to force their foodstuffs on an unwilling people.
The country is labouring under a great tremendous debt, and there is only one reasonable way in which this debt can be paid off, namely, by increasingly making use of the natural resources and raw materials of the country-developing them and selling them on the world's market. Sometimes in the spring of the year a gardener or farmer will sow seeds in a hotbed and when the plants get old enough to be able to stand out in the open they are immediately moved out there. It often saves time and speeds up the process of growing vegetables to do that; but no vegetable grower or farmer will leave those seeds in the hotbed and expect that they will mature there and reach a profitable or useful growth. By giving a little assistance to new settlers, as well as to old settlers in the country, you will bring these newer lands to which I have referred under cultivation. This will be a good thing for the people who go on these lands and for the Dominion, and will help materially in producing the extra wealth which this country needs to carry its present load. It will also make for greater development all round- greater development for business men and for manufacturers, as well as for the farmers themselves. I feel that this scheme should apply particularly to the five provinces I have named, as well as British Columbia. I am not so familiar with the natural resources or
the vacant lands of the Maritime provinces, but if there is any way in which they can be put to better use than at present, personally I am in favour of it, and I think everyone else on this side of the House would take the same view.

If this resolution upon
which the bill is to be founded had for its object the assisting of settlers to clear land in the areas which I indicated some time ago, there .might be something to be said in its favour. I have listened to the debate and have asked one or two questions in an attempt to find out in what way the settler could secure assistance for the clearing of his land through this particular resolution or the bill which is subsequently to be founded upon it. Frankly I have been disappointed in not being able to secure that information. The hon. member for Brandon said that the settler would work at harvest and threshing in the summer and spend the winter on the homestead. What will he do in the winter on these lands? Will he cut pulpwood? I tried to find out from the minister just after dinner where these lands were, what class of lands they were, and whether or not those in Saskatchewan or the prairie provinces were heavily timbered. If the lands in British Columbia along the existing lines of railway are proposed to be cleared, I may tell the committee that the cost of clearing them will run from $100 an acre up, and the settler will have to expend a large amount of money before he can get the loan at all. If you take sections of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, particularly the northern sections along the branch lines of the Canadian National railway and some portions of the Canadian Pacific railway, you will find that while you have not so much of the heavy timber, you have a considerable portion of it. You have some very good land, I have no doubt, but you will have to pay for the clearing of it. If the location of these lands is where my recollection tells me they are and where the minister indicates they are, it will cost in some cases not $5 an acre but close to $15 an acre, and perhaps even more. I think the minister, who knows the situation, will bear me out in that statement. In the case of the settler coming in there without any money, the labourer working for wages on farms in the west, how is it possible for him to clear that land at a cost of $10, $12 or $15 an acre, build his home, and in general place himself in a position to avail himself of this loan within a year, or, as the hon. minister says, within two years or three years?
